saints.bio: Soldier who, per Pope Damasus's epitaph, quit the army for Christ. Martyred with Nereus, buried on the Via Ardeatina.
Vojtěch, Bishop of Prague, who went as a missionary to the pagan Prussians and was killed by them in 997.
Virgin of Catania who refused a Roman official and died after torture under Decius. Named in the Roman Canon.
Roman girl martyred at 12 or 13 for her vow to Christ. Named in the Roman Canon; lambs are blessed on her feast.
Dominican friar, Bishop of Regensburg, teacher of Thomas Aquinas. Philosopher, naturalist, the Universal Doctor.
Gonzaga heir who renounced his inheritance to become a Jesuit. Died at 23 after nursing plague victims in Rome.
Naples lawyer turned priest and bishop. Founded the Redemptorists, wrote The Glories of Mary, patron of confessors.
Governor acclaimed Bishop of Milan while still a catechumen. Hymn writer, baptizer of Augustine, rebuker of an emperor.
Fisherman of Bethsaida and disciple of John the Baptist, the First-Called. Brought his brother Simon Peter to Jesus.
Vietnamese priest, ransomed, rearrested and beheaded in Hanoi in 1839. First named of the 117 Vietnamese Martyrs.
First Korean-born Catholic priest, ordained in Shanghai. Beheaded by the Han River in Seoul in 1846, aged 25.
Franciscan tertiary of Brescia who founded the Company of St Ursula in 1535, the root of the Ursulines.
Mother of the Virgin Mary, wife of Joachim, grandmother of Jesus. Her name comes from the Protoevangelium of James.
Monk and abbot of Bec, Archbishop of Canterbury. Faith seeking understanding: the Proslogion and Cur Deus Homo.
Monk of Corbie, Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, Apostle of the North. Preached in Denmark and at Birka in Sweden.
Catalan weaver turned priest. Founded the Claretians, Archbishop of Santiago de Cuba, confessor to Queen Isabella II.
Egyptian who sold all and went into the desert. Father of monks, tempted by demons; his Life was written by Athanasius.
Lisbon-born Franciscan whose preaching moved Italy. Evangelical Doctor, wonderworker, finder of lost things.
Cremona physician turned priest. Founded the Barnabites and Angelic Sisters; spread Eucharistic adoration in Milan.
First Bishop of Ravenna, by tradition sent by St Peter. Shown in the apse mosaic of Sant'Apollinare in Classe.
Bishop of Alexandria, exiled five times for defending Nicaea against Arius. Wrote On the Incarnation and Life of Antony.
Prior of St Andrew's in Rome, sent by Gregory the Great to the English in 597. First Archbishop of Canterbury.
Rhetor from Thagaste, baptized by Ambrose in 387, then Bishop of Hippo. Wrote the Confessions and The City of God.
Chinese soldier converted while guarding a captive missionary. Became a priest; died in prison in Chengdu in 1815.
Levite of Cyprus, son of consolation. Vouched for Paul in Jerusalem and went with him on the first mission.
One of the Twelve, often identified with Nathanael of Cana. Tradition says he was flayed alive in Armenia.
Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Monastic lawgiver, defender of the Holy Spirit, builder of a hospital for the poor.
Monk of Wearmouth-Jarrow. Wrote the Ecclesiastical History of the English People and popularized AD dating.
Father of Western monasticism. Hermit at Subiaco, founder of Monte Cassino, author of the Rule. Patron of Europe.
Cistercian abbot of Clairvaux, the Mellifluous Doctor. Sermons on the Song of Songs; preached the Second Crusade.
Franciscan preacher who crossed Italy holding up a tablet of the IHS. Apostle of the Holy Name of Jesus.
Bishop of Sebaste, martyred in 316. Healed a boy choking on a fish bone; throats are blessed with crossed candles.
Mother of God, full of grace. Said yes at Nazareth, stood by the Cross, prayed with the Apostles in the Upper Room.
Franciscan Minister General and Cardinal-Bishop of Albano. The Seraphic Doctor; wrote The Journey of the Mind into God.
Wynfrith of Wessex, Apostle of the Germans. Felled Donar's Oak, organized the German Church, martyred in Frisia in 754.
Swedish noblewoman and mother of eight. Mystic of the Revelations, founder of the Bridgettines, co-patroness of Europe.
Head of the cathedral school of Reims who sought solitude. Founded the Carthusians at Chartreuse in 1084.
Vicenza-born priest who co-founded the Theatines in 1524 to reform the clergy, and a bank to free the poor from usurers.
Former slave who became Bishop of Rome. Ran the cemetery on the Appian Way that bears his name; welcomed penitents back.
Soldier and gambler turned nurse and priest. Founded the Camillians, Ministers of the Sick, marked by a red cross.
Jagiellonian prince, son of King Casimir IV and heir to the throne. Died at 25 in Grodno; patron of Lithuania.
Learned virgin of Alexandria who, by tradition, out-argued pagan philosophers. Condemned to the wheel, then beheaded.
Dominican tertiary and mystic. Wrote the Dialogue and urged the pope to leave Avignon for Rome. Patroness of Italy.
Roman virgin martyr named in the Roman Canon. Her Acts say she sang to God in her heart as music played at her wedding.
Cardinal Archbishop of Milan. Put Trent's reforms into practice, founded seminaries, stayed with his flock in plague.
Chief of the royal pages of Buganda. Shielded the boys in his care and was burned alive at Namugongo in 1886.
Mexican parish priest who ran a clandestine seminary. Shot without trial in 1927 after absolving his executioners.
Noblewoman of Assisi who followed Francis into poverty. Founded the Poor Clares; faced invaders with the Eucharist.
Early Bishop of Rome whose Letter to the Corinthians survives. Tradition says he was drowned with an anchor in Crimea.
Irish monk of Bangor who crossed to Gaul. Founded Luxeuil and Bobbio, wrote a stern Rule and frank letters to popes.
Bishop of Rome from 251. Readmitted the repentant lapsed against Novatian's rigorism; died in exile at Centumcellae.
Physician who, with his twin Damian, healed without taking fees. Martyred under Diocletian; named in the Roman Canon.
Rhetorician turned Bishop of Carthage. Wrote On the Unity of the Church; beheaded under Valerian in 258.

saints.n: St. Cyril, Apostle of the Slavs
saints.bio: Constantine the Philosopher of Thessalonica. With Methodius gave the Slavs letters and liturgy; died a monk in Rome.
Patriarch of Alexandria. Defended Mary as Theotokos, Mother of God, against Nestorius at Ephesus in 431.
Bishop of Jerusalem, exiled three times in the Arian strife. His Catechetical Lectures prepared converts for baptism.
Bishop of Rome 366-384. Set Jerome to revise the Latin Bible and honored the martyrs with verses carved on their tombs.
Physician who, with his twin Cosmas, healed without taking fees. Martyred under Diocletian; named in the Roman Canon.
First Bishop of Paris. Beheaded at Montmartre with Rusticus and Eleutherius; one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers.
Castilian canon who preached against the Albigensian heresy and founded the Order of Preachers. Died at Bologna, 1221.
Hungarian princess, Landgravine of Thuringia. Widowed at 20, she spent herself on the sick poor at Marburg; dead at 24.
Aragonese princess, Queen of Portugal. Peacemaker between warring kings; widowed, a Franciscan tertiary at Coimbra.
Deacon of Nisibis and Edessa. Taught the faith in Syriac hymns and verse, earning the name Harp of the Holy Spirit.
First Bishop of Vercelli. Lived in community with his clergy; exiled east for refusing to condemn Athanasius.
Layman made Bishop of Rome in 236 when a dove settled on his head. Organized the deacons; martyred under Decius.
Polish Sister of Our Lady of Mercy. Mystic whose Diary spread the Divine Mercy image and chaplet. Canonized in 2000.
Slave and catechumen of Carthage. Gave birth in prison, then faced the beasts in the arena beside Perpetua in 203.
Lawyer known as the poor man's advocate, then Capuchin friar. Killed while preaching in Calvinist Graubünden, 1622.
Roman noblewoman, wife and mother. Nursed the poor through plague and war; founded the Oblates of Tor de' Specchi.
Bishop of Geneva. Won back the Chablais with sermons and leaflets; wrote Introduction to the Devout Life.
Merchant's son wedded to Lady Poverty. Founded the Friars Minor, wrote the Canticle of the Sun, bore the stigmata.
Calabrian hermit, founder of the Minims. Kept a perpetual Lent; called to France to the deathbed of Louis XI.
Navarrese Jesuit, early companion of Ignatius. Preached from Goa to Japan; died on Shangchuan Island off China, 1552.
I am Gabriel, who stand before God. Sent to Daniel, to Zachary, and to Mary at Nazareth: Hail, full of grace.
Soldier martyred under Diocletian, venerated at Lydda. The dragon-slayer of legend; patron of knights and England.
Nun of Helfta from childhood. Mystic of the Heart of Jesus; her Herald of Divine Love records her visions.
Prefect, monk, then pope 590-604. Sent Augustine to England, wrote the Pastoral Rule; servant of the servants of God.
Cappadocian poet-bishop called the Theologian. His Theological Orations defended the Trinity at Constantinople.
Armenian monk of Narek. His Book of Lamentations, prayer from the depths of the heart, made him a Doctor in 2015.
Hildebrand of Sovana, pope 1073-1085. Fought lay investiture, met Henry IV at Canossa, died in exile at Salerno.
Bavarian-born Duchess of Silesia. Founded Trzebnica Abbey, cared for the poor and sick, and spent her widowhood there.
Last Ottonian king, Holy Roman Emperor from 1014. Founded the see of Bamberg and backed reform of the Church.
Convert from paganism, Bishop of Poitiers. Exiled to Phrygia, wrote On the Trinity; the Athanasius of the West.
Benedictine abbess of the Rhineland. Visionary of Scivias, composer, medical writer, counselor of popes and emperors.
Learned Roman priest who opposed Pope Callistus. Exiled to Sardinia's mines with Pope Pontian, he died reconciled.
Bishop of Antioch taken in chains to Rome for the beasts. His letters hold the earliest known use of Catholic Church.
Basque soldier converted on his sickbed after Pamplona. Wrote the Spiritual Exercises and founded the Society of Jesus.
Hearer of Polycarp, Bishop of Lyon. Refuted the Gnostics in Against Heresies; declared Doctor of Unity in 2022.
French Jesuit missionary to the Huron. Captured and maimed by the Mohawk, he escaped, returned, and was killed in 1646.
Archbishop of Seville. Compiled the Etymologies, an encyclopedia of ancient learning; presided at Toledo IV in 633.
Son of Zebedee, brother of John, a Son of Thunder. First apostle martyred, by Herod's sword; venerated at Compostela.
Widowed Burgundian baroness and mother. With Francis de Sales founded the Visitation of Holy Mary at Annecy in 1610.
Bishop of Benevento, beheaded near Pozzuoli under Diocletian. His blood, kept in Naples, is famed for liquefying.
Venetian officer freed from captivity, turned father of orphans. Founded the Somascans; died nursing the sick in plague.
Dalmatian scholar, secretary to Pope Damasus, then monk at Bethlehem. Translated the Bible into Latin: the Vulgate.
Husband of St. Anne and father of the Virgin Mary, known by name from the 2nd-century Protoevangelium of James.
Son of Zebedee, the disciple whom Jesus loved. Took Mary into his home; Gospel, three letters, and the Apocalypse.

saints.n: St. John Baptist de la Salle
saints.bio: Canon of Reims who gave up wealth and rank to found the Brothers of the Christian Schools. Patron of teachers.
Turin priest who gathered street boys into his Oratory and founded the Salesians. Reason, religion, loving-kindness.
Golden-mouthed preacher of Antioch, then Archbishop of Constantinople. Rebuked the court's luxury and died in exile.
Monk of Mar Saba from Damascus. Defended the holy icons against the iconoclasts; wrote The Fount of Knowledge.
Norman Jesuit, missionary to the Huron, credited with the Huron Carol. Tortured to death by the Iroquois, 1649.
Norman priest and mission preacher. Founded the Eudists; apostle of the Hearts of Jesus and Mary.
Bishop of Rochester, made cardinal in prison. Would not accept Henry VIII as head of the Church; beheaded, 1535.
Anglican priest who became a Catholic, Oratorian and cardinal. Wrote the Apologia; named Doctor of the Church in 2025.
Tuscan pope sent by Theodoric to Constantinople. Jailed by the Arian king at Ravenna on his return; died there, 526.
Pharmacist's apprentice turned priest in Lucca. Founded the Clerks Regular of the Mother of God.
Curé of Ars. Heard confessions up to 16 hours a day as pilgrims poured into his small village.
Apostle of Andalusia. His preaching converted John of God; he counselled Teresa of Ávila. Doctor of the Church, 2012.
Lawyer, then Franciscan preacher. At 70 he rallied the crusaders who broke the Ottoman siege of Belgrade, 1456.
Portuguese soldier and bookseller turned servant of the sick poor in Granada. Founder of the Brothers Hospitallers.
Kraków professor and priest. Walked to Rome on pilgrimage, gave his clothes and money to the poor.
Carmelite friar, poet and mystic who reformed the Carmelites with Teresa. Dark Night of the Soul, Spiritual Canticle.
Karol Wojtyła of Kraków. Pope for 26 years, pilgrim to 129 countries. Be not afraid. Totus tuus.
Angelo Roncalli, sharecroppers' son from Bergamo. Called the Second Vatican Council. The Good Pope.
Basilian monk and Ruthenian Catholic Archbishop of Polotsk. Worked for union with Rome; killed by a mob at Vitebsk.
Aragonese priest who opened free schools for Rome's poor children in 1597. Founder of the Piarists.
Husband of Mary, foster father of Jesus, carpenter of Nazareth. A just man; the Gospels record not one word of his.
The carpenter of Nazareth, whose trade Jesus shared. May Day feast set by Pius XII in 1955 for the dignity of labor.
Kidnapped into slavery as a child in Sudan, freed in Italy, she became a Canossian sister and died at Schio.
Nahua layman. Our Lady of Guadalupe appeared to him at Tepeyac in 1531; her image appeared on his tilma.
Apostle, also called Thaddeus. At the Last Supper asked why Jesus would show himself to them and not to the world.
Philosopher from Samaria who found in Christ the true philosophy. Wrote the Apologies; beheaded in Rome.
Capuchin preacher and linguist. Led imperial troops, crucifix in hand, against the Turks in 1601. The Apostolic Doctor.
Deacon of Pope Sixtus II. Showed the poor as the Church's treasure; martyred in 258, by tradition on a gridiron.
Chinese-Filipino layman of Binondo, Manila, husband and father. Martyred at Nagasaki in 1637; the first Filipino saint.
Brother of Martha and Mary, friend of Jesus. Four days in the tomb, then called out alive: Lazarus, come forth.
Pope 440 to 461. His Tome on Christ's two natures was hailed at Chalcedon; met Attila in 452.
Itinerant preacher of western France. True Devotion to Mary, Secret of the Rosary; founded the Montfort Missionaries.
King of France. Built the Sainte-Chapelle for the Crown of Thorns, fed the poor at his table, died on crusade at Tunis.
Virgin of Syracuse who gave her dowry to the poor and was martyred under Diocletian. Her name means light.
Paul's most dear physician and companion. Wrote the Third Gospel, with the Magnificat and the Prodigal Son, and Acts.
Roman priest beheaded with Peter the exorcist under Diocletian. Both are named in the Roman Canon.
Visitation nun of Paray-le-Monial. Her visions of the Sacred Heart spread the First Fridays and the Holy Hour.
English princess, Queen of Scots, wife of Malcolm III. Fed orphans and the poor daily; founded a priory at Dunfermline.
Farm girl of 11, stabbed resisting Alessandro Serenelli in 1902. Forgave him as she died; he later repented.
Author of the Second Gospel, cousin of Barnabas, Peter's interpreter. By tradition founder of the Church of Alexandria.
Hostess of Jesus at Bethany, sister of Mary and Lazarus. Confessed him the Christ, the Son of God, when Lazarus died.
Dominican brother of Lima, son of a Spaniard and a freed slave. Barber, healer, friend of the poor and of animals.
Pope who condemned Monothelitism at the Lateran Synod of 649. Arrested by the emperor, exiled to Crimea; died there.
Soldier who cut his cloak in half for a beggar at Amiens. Monk, then Bishop of Tours; father of Gallic monasticism.
Of Magdala. Followed Jesus, stood by the Cross, first to see him risen. Apostle to the Apostles.
Florentine Carmelite mystic. Her sisters wrote down the words she spoke in ecstasy; endured five years of desolation.
Sister of Martha and Lazarus. Sat at the Lord's feet and chose the best part; anointed him with costly spikenard.
Tax collector who left his booth when Jesus said Follow me. Apostle and author of the First Gospel.
Disciple from John's baptism to the Ascension, chosen by lot to take Judas's place among the Twelve (Acts 1).
Polish Franciscan, founder of the Militia Immaculatae. At Auschwitz he took a condemned father's place and died, 1941.
Brother of Cyril, from Thessalonica. Apostle of the Slavs, Archbishop of Sirmium; brought Slavonic liturgy to Moravia.
Archangel whose name asks Who is like God? Leads heaven's host against the dragon (Apoc. 12). Guardian of the Church.
Mother of Augustine. Prayed and wept for his conversion for years; died at Ostia in 387, soon after his baptism.
Soldier who, per Pope Damasus, threw down his arms for Christ. Martyred with Achilleus; buried in Domitilla's catacomb.
Bishop of Myra in Lycia, said to have secretly paid three poor girls' dowries. Wonderworker, the source of Santa Claus.
Canon of Xanten converted when lightning threw him from his horse. Founded the Norbertines; Archbishop of Magdeburg.
By tradition a Phrygian orphan, baptized in Rome and beheaded at 14 under Diocletian. Buried on the Via Aurelia.
Briton enslaved in Ireland as a youth. Escaped, returned as bishop to win the island for Christ. Wrote the Confessio.
Pharisee of Tarsus turned Apostle of the Gentiles on the Damascus road. Letters, journeys, shipwreck; beheaded in Rome.
Son of a martyr, lay leader of Korea's hidden Church. Went to Beijing to plead for priests; martyred in Seoul, 1839.
Japanese Jesuit preacher, crucified at Nagasaki in 1597 with 25 companions. Forgave his executioners from the cross.
Founder of the Passionists, vowed to keep Christ's Passion in memory. A famed preacher of parish missions in Italy.
Giovanni Battista Montini. Closed Vatican II, laid his tiara on the altar for the poor, wrote Humanae Vitae.
Wealthy ex-consul from Bordeaux who gave away his fortune. Bishop of Nola, Christian poet, friend of Augustine.
Young noblewoman and nursing mother of Carthage. Kept a prison diary before dying in the arena with Felicity in 203.
Fisherman Jesus named the Rock. Denied Him thrice, professed his love thrice, led the Apostles, died in Rome.
Dutch Jesuit, Second Apostle of Germany. His catechisms renewed Catholic life in German lands after the Reformation.
Marist priest from rural France sent to the Pacific island of Futuna. Killed there in 1841, the first martyr of Oceania.
Bishop of Ravenna whose brief, golden sermons earned him the name Chrysologus. Doctor of the Church.
Jesuit at Cartagena's slave port who signed himself servant of the Africans forever. Met the ships with food and care.
Hermit of Fonte Avellana, made Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia. Fierce foe of simony and clerical vice. Doctor of the Church.
Apostle of the Eucharist. Marist priest who founded the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament for perpetual adoration.
Roman exorcist beheaded with the priest Marcellinus under Diocletian. Damasus heard their story from the executioner.
Apostle from Bethsaida. Told Nathanael Come and see; at the Last Supper asked Jesus to show them the Father.
Florentine who became the Apostle of Rome. Founded the Oratory, felt his heart set ablaze, prized humility and joy.
Capuchin friar of San Giovanni Rotondo. Bore the stigmata 50 years, spent long hours confessing, built a hospital.
Dominican pope who carried out Trent: 1570 Missal, Breviary, Catechism. Forged the Holy League that won at Lepanto.
Son of a village postman. Motto: to restore all things in Christ. Opened Communion to children, fought Modernism.
Bishop of Smyrna who knew John the Apostle. After 86 years serving Christ, refused to revile Him; burned and stabbed.
Pope exiled to Sardinia's mines by Maximinus Thrax. First pope to resign, in 235, so Rome could elect a successor.
Archangel of the Book of Tobit. Guided Tobias, bound the demon, healed Tobit's eyes. His name means God heals.
Catalan Dominican canonist. Compiled the Decretals of Gregory IX and served as Master of his Order. Lived to about 100.
Wife, mother, widow, then Augustinian nun of Cascia. Bore a thorn wound on her forehead. Patroness of impossible causes.
Jesuit cardinal and theologian. His Controversies answered the Reformers point by point; his catechisms taught children.
Ravenna noble who did penance after his father killed a kinsman in a duel. Founded the Camaldolese hermit-monks.
Dominican tertiary of Lima, first canonized saint of the Americas. Prayed in a garden hermitage; nursed the sick poor.
Sister of St. Benedict, vowed to God from childhood. Her prayer called down a storm to keep him talking one last night.
Roman soldier under Diocletian. By tradition shot with arrows, survived, then was beaten to death for confessing Christ.
Maronite monk of Lebanon. Spent his last 23 years as a hermit at Annaya in silence, prayer and fasting. Wonderworker.
Simon the Zealot, one of the Twelve. Tradition says he preached with Jude in Persia and was martyred there, sawn in two.
Pope seized while teaching in a catacomb under Valerian and beheaded with his deacons. Lawrence died four days later.
Bishop of Kraków who rebuked King Bolesław II and was slain by him, by tradition while saying Mass. Patron of Poland.
First King of Hungary, crowned in 1000 or 1001. Founded dioceses and built up the Church. His right hand is enshrined.
One of the first seven deacons, full of grace and fortitude. Stoned outside Jerusalem as Saul looked on; died forgiving.
Bishop of Rome for most of Constantine's reign, as persecution gave way to basilicas. Sent legates to Nicaea.

saints.n: St. Teresa Benedicta of the Cross
saints.bio: Edith Stein. Jewish-born philosopher and Husserl's assistant, then Carmelite nun. Killed at Auschwitz, 1942.
Albanian nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta for the poorest of the poor. Nobel Peace Prize, 1979.
Carmelite reformer of Ávila. Founded Discalced convents, wrote The Interior Castle. First woman Doctor of the Church.
Carmelite of Lisieux, dead of tuberculosis at 24. Her Little Way and Story of a Soul made her a Doctor of the Church.
Didymus, the Twin. Doubted the Resurrection until shown the wounds: My Lord, and my God. By tradition, Apostle of India.
Dominican friar, the Angelic Doctor. Wrote the Summa Theologiae and the Corpus Christi office; at last called it straw.
Henry II's chancellor, then Archbishop of Canterbury. Upheld Church rights; slain by four knights in his own cathedral.
Lawyer, author of Utopia, Lord Chancellor. Would not swear to Henry VIII's supremacy over the Church; beheaded in 1535.
Paul's beloved son in faith, from Lystra, taught by his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois. First Bishop of Ephesus.
Gentile convert, Paul's companion at Jerusalem and envoy to Corinth. Left in Crete to ordain priests; its first bishop.
Salamanca law teacher, then Archbishop of Lima. Walked his vast see, issued a Quechua catechism, confirmed Rose of Lima.
Gascon farm boy turned Paris priest. Founded the Vincentians and, with Louise de Marillac, the Daughters of Charity.
Valencian Dominican whose preaching tours stirred Europe for 20 years. Labored to end the Western Schism.
Deacon and voice of Saragossa's stammering bishop. Racked and roasted on a gridiron at Valencia under Dacian.
Duke of Bohemia, schooled in the faith by grandmother Ludmila. Slain by brother Boleslaus's men. Good King Wenceslas.

saints.n: The Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church
saints.bio: Mother of all Christian people, as Paul VI proclaimed at Vatican II in 1964. Memorial on Pentecost Monday since 2018.
Romano-British martyr of Caerleon, put to death with Julius. With Alban, the only named martyrs of Roman Britain.
Burgundian princess, queen of Italy, then wife of Otto I and Holy Roman Empress. Regent for Otto III; died at Selz.
Sister of St. Vitalis of Savigny and first abbess of the Abbaye Blanche at Mortain, a nunnery of the Savigny reform.
Fifth-century Bishop of Metz, tenth in its list. Louis the Pious moved his relics to Neuwiller in Alsace in 826.
Mother of St. Gerald of Aurillac, named in Odo of Cluny's Life of Gerald. Venerated in the Diocese of Saint-Flour.
Steward at King David I's Scottish court turned Cistercian abbot of Rievaulx. Wrote Spiritual Friendship.
Óengus the Culdee, monk-bishop of Tallaght. Credited with the Félire, the earliest metrical martyrology in a vernacular.
Styled Bishop of Comminges and remembered for zeal for orthodoxy. Died in the Rouergue; his tomb was at Saint-Affrique.
Companion of Agoard, slain with him and a crowd of fellow Christians at Créteil near Paris. Relics in Saint-Christophe.
Widowed catechist from Guizhou sent by Fr. Chapdelaine to teach the faith in Guangxi. Jailed with him; died in a cage.
Czech princess who turned down Emperor Frederick II, founded Prague's Poor Clares and the Knights of the Red Star.
Martyr of Créteil near Paris, slain with Aglibert and companions beyond counting. Usuard's martyrology tells the tale.
Máedóc, or Mogue, pupil of St. David in Wales. Founded the monastery of Ferns and became first bishop there.
Iona monk sent at King Oswald's call to evangelize Northumbria. Founded Lindisfarne; the king translated his sermons.
Pre-Patrician saint of Munster, founder and first bishop of Emly. Legend says a she-wolf suckled him as a foundling.
Patron of Lavaur in the Tarn, whose co-cathedral bears his name. Little is known; held to be a 7th-century bishop.
Verulamium man who hid a fleeing priest, put on his cloak, and was beheaded in his place. Britain's first martyr.
PIME missionary priest from Altavilla Irpina, in southern Shaanxi from 1888. Killed in the Boxer Rising, 1900.
Lost a leg in the 1863 Uprising, won fame as a painter, then left art for Kraków's homeless. Founded the Albertines.
Chilean Jesuit trained in law. Founded Hogar de Cristo for the homeless in 1944, a union federation and Mensaje.
Breton abbot of Tintillac, made Bishop of Angers in 529. Fought incestuous noble marriages; Fortunatus wrote his Life.
Greek Christian of Lyon and friend of Epipodius. Seized with him under Marcus Aurelius, scourged, then crucified.
Bishop of Cahors, honored on July 4 with Sts. Florent and Urcisse and all the holy bishops of that see.
The sainted bishops of Angers, among them Maurilius, Albinus and Licinius, honored together in one diocesan memorial.

saints.n: The Holy Bishops of Beauvais, Noyon and Senlis
saints.bio: Sainted bishops of the three sees now joined in the Diocese of Beauvais, such as Medard and Eligius of Noyon.
The sainted bishops of Cahors, such as Desiderius, kept together with Florent, Alithe and Urcisse on July 4.

saints.n: The Holy Bishops of Coutances and Avranches
saints.bio: Sainted bishops of Coutances and Avranches, like Laud and Aubert, founder of Mont-Saint-Michel. Kept with its priests.
The sainted bishops of Mende in the Gévaudan, among them the martyr Privatus, honored with St. Firmin on January 14.

saints.n: The Holy Priests of Coutances and Avranches
saints.bio: The holy priests of the Diocese of Coutances and Avranches in Normandy, kept in one memorial with its sainted bishops.
Every saint of the island of saints and scholars, from Patrick, Brigid and Columba to the many never named.
All the saints and blesseds tied to the Archdiocese of Lille in French Flanders, honored together each November 8.
All the saints of the Church of Paris, from Denis and Genevieve to Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac.

saints.n: The Saints of Beauvais, Noyon and Senlis
saints.bio: All the saints of the Diocese of Beauvais, Noyon and Senlis in the Oise, honored together each November 8.

saints.n: The Saints of Coutances and Avranches
saints.bio: All the saints of the Diocese of Coutances and Avranches in the Manche, Normandy, honored together each November 8.
All the saints of the Diocese of Créteil southeast of Paris, among them its martyrs Agoard and Aglibert.

saints.n: The Saints of Gap and Embrun
saints.bio: All the saints of the Alpine Diocese of Gap and Embrun, from Marcellinus, first bishop of Embrun, to Arnulf of Gap.
All the saints of the Diocese of Nanterre west of Paris, among them Genevieve, born at Nanterre.
All the saints of the Diocese of Nîmes in the Gard, among them the martyr Baudilus and Giles of Saint-Gilles.
All the saints of the Diocese of Saint-Denis north of Paris, first among them Denis, whose basilica is its cathedral.
Every saint of Wales, from David, Teilo and Dyfrig to Winefride and the Welsh martyrs of the Reformation.
Led the first Salesian mission to China, then first Vicar Apostolic of Shiuchow. Killed by pirates shielding girls.
Monk of Deerhurst, Bishop of Winchester, Archbishop of Canterbury. Seized by Danes, he forbade a ransom and was killed.

saints.n: St. Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception
saints.bio: Franciscan Clarist sister of Kerala who offered years of illness as a sacrifice. First woman of Indian origin canonized.
Spanish Jesuit of the Paraguay missions, killed with St. Roque González at Caaró in 1628. Martyr of the Río de la Plata.
Priest and companion of St. Martial, first Bishop of Limoges. The Martyrology says their lives shone with miracles.
Augustine's closest friend: converted alongside him, baptized with him by Ambrose in 387, then Bishop of Thagaste.
Missionary monk in Flanders, briefly Bishop of Maastricht, founder of the abbey of Elnone, later called Saint-Amand.
First known Bishop of Strasbourg, attested about the year 346.
First Bishop of Rodez, his life glorious for holiness and miracles. Principal patron of the Diocese of Rodez.
Martyr buried at Albi when his faithful contending was over, per the Roman Martyrology. Alive for evermore in glory.
Abbot slain with St. Praejectus, Bishop of Clermont, in the 670s. The Saint-Amarin valley in Alsace bears his name.
Azorean priest in Rio Grande do Norte, killed with his flock by a Dutch-led force at Uruaçu in 1645. Martyr of Natal.
Monk born in Venice who ended his days in the County of Foix. His relics drew pilgrims to Saint-Martin-d'Oydes.
Holy Cross brother and porter in Montreal whose devotion to St. Joseph drew the sick and built St. Joseph's Oratory.
Alsatian Franciscan lay brother at the Taiyuan mission, killed by the Boxers on 9 July 1900. A Martyr of China.
Jesuit preacher, the Apostle of Lithuania, tortured to death by Cossacks at Janów in 1657. Patron of Poland.
Brazilian-born priest of Cunhaú, killed with his people while saying Mass on 16 July 1645. One of the Martyrs of Natal.
Poitou parish priest who fled the Revolution, then ministered in secret. Co-founded the Daughters of the Cross.
Polish-born Benedictine of Zobor who became a hermit by the Váh with his disciple Benedict. Patron of Nitra.
Abbess of Oroër near Beauvais. Legend says leprosy freed her from a betrothal to St. Ansbert. Patroness of Beauvais.
Widow who kept safe houses for hunted priests. Hanged at Tyburn in 1601, wishing she could have sheltered a thousand.
Carmelite of Compiègne, Sister Marie-Henriette of Providence. Guillotined in Paris with her community on 17 July 1794.
Archbishop of Cologne who seized young Henry IV at Kaiserswerth in 1062 and ruled as regent. Founder of Siegburg Abbey.
Franciscan from Trevi in Umbria, Vicar Apostolic of Southern Hunan from 1892. Killed by rioters at Hengyang in 1900.
Hermit and martyr honored at Lialores near Condom in Gascony, where a Romanesque church bears his name.

saints.n: St. Anthony of Saint Anne Galvão
saints.bio: Franciscan friar of São Paulo who built the Luz monastery and gave out paper prayer pills. First Brazilian-born saint.
Hermit trained on Mount Athos who settled in a cave at Kiev and, with Theodosius, founded the Kiev Caves Lavra.
Martyr venerated as patron of Pamiers; his relics are honored at Palencia in Spain. His history is uncertain.
Bishop of Strasbourg famed for miracles. By his own wish he was buried outside the city, near the gallows.
Bishop of Gap in the Alps around the year 600, born at Chalon-sur-Saône. Known in France as St. Arey.
Abbot of Lézat in the Ariège, honored in the proper calendar of the Diocese of Pamiers.
Noble-born monk of La Trinité at Vendôme, sent from Rome to be Bishop of Gap about 1065. Patron of the city and diocese.
Disciple of St. Kentigern, said to have carried him live coals unburnt. Bishop of Llanelwy, now the city of St Asaph.
St. Patrick's coppersmith, maker of chalices, patens and book covers, and first Bishop of Elphin. Patron of Elphin.
First abbess of St. Stephen's in Strasbourg, the convent founded by her father, Duke Adalbert. Niece of St. Odile.
Irish virgin who founded a hostel for travellers at Killaraght on Lough Gara. It served wayfarers until 1539.
Bishop of Avranches who, at St. Michael's bidding in 708, raised the first sanctuary on Mont-Saint-Michel.
Courtier of King Dagobert, co-founder of Rebais Abbey, Bishop of Rouen from 641. Friend and biographer of St. Eligius.
Monk of Luxeuil made Bishop of Thérouanne in 637. Founded Sithiu abbey with St. Bertin; Saint-Omer is named for him.
Deacon of Tarragona burned alive in 259 with Bishop Fructuosus and Deacon Eulogius, arms stretched out in prayer.
Paris Foreign Missions priest in Guangxi, caged and executed in 1856. France used his death as a pretext for war.
Roman virgin martyr, by tradition slain under Valerian. Relics of hers reached Monaco in 1641; a patroness of Monaco.
By legend a companion of St. Ursula who died of fever at Strasbourg. Her tomb drew pilgrims seeking cures for fevers.
Bordeaux-born abbot of Saint-Orens, then Archbishop of Auch from 1049. A leader of the Gregorian reform in Gascony.
Apostle of Auvergne and first Bishop of Clermont, one of seven bishops sent to Gaul from Rome per Gregory of Tours.
Pyrenean hermit of the Larboust valley, beheaded by Saracens in legend. The village of Saint-Aventin bears his name.
Locksmith of Lyon who gave even his tools to the poor, then a subdeacon at Saint-Just. Also called Galmier.
Virgin martyr of legend, shut in a tower by her father, who beheaded her himself. Invoked against lightning.
Dominican Archbishop of Braga, reformer at the Council of Trent, author of Stimulus Pastorum on the duties of bishops.
Wife of St. Julian, with whom she lived in virginity, sheltering clergy in the persecution. She died in peace.
Martyr of Nîmes who refused to sacrifice to the gods and held firm under torture. Hailed as the true apostle of Nîmes.
Portuguese noblewoman at the Castilian court who withdrew to Toledo and founded the Conceptionist nuns.
The Second Benedict. Left Charlemagne's court for the cloister and bound Frankish monasteries to the Benedictine Rule.

saints.n: St. Benedict of Jesus Valdivielso Sáez
saints.bio: Buenos Aires-born De La Salle Brother, shot with the Martyrs of Turón in 1934. Argentina's first saint.
Monk of Zobor, then cave hermit near Trenčín with his master Andrew Zorard. Killed by robbers in 1012.
Son of African slaves in Sicily. Hermit, then Franciscan lay brother and cook, chosen guardian of his Palermo friary.
Shepherd boy who, by tradition, set the first stone of the bridge over the Rhône at Avignon. Patron of bridge builders.
Brother of the Christian Schools. Spent twenty years teaching the boys of Saugues, with evening classes for adults.
Bishop of Meissen for forty years. Shown with a fish holding the cathedral keys. Patron of Munich.
Franciscan sent by Francis to Morocco. Beheaded at Marrakesh in 1220 with four friars, the Order's first martyrs.
Benedictine monk of Saint-Papoul in Languedoc: novice master, almoner and master of works. Died in 1093.
Miller's daughter of Lourdes who saw the Lady at Massabielle in 1858. Later a Sister of Charity at Nevers.
Abbot of Montsalvy in Auvergne after its founder, St. Gausbert. Patron of the town, where his reliquary is kept.
Hermit, abbot and reformer. Founded Tiron Abbey in the Perche, mother house of the Tironensian monks.
Bishop of Comminges who rebuilt its cathedral with a Romanesque cloister. The hilltop town now bears his name.
Welsh abbot of Clynnog Fawr. Tradition says he restored his niece St. Winefride to life.
Slave girl among the martyrs of Lyon, 177. Scourged, roasted and tossed by a bull, she outlasted them all.
Son of Vladimir the Great. Would not raise arms against his brother and was killed in 1015. A passion-bearer, with Gleb.
Abbot of Clonfert. The Navigator: the Voyage of St. Brendan sails him across the ocean in search of the Promised Land.
Abbess of Kildare and co-patroness of Ireland with Patrick and Columba. Her cross is still woven on her feast.
Saxon noble, monk and missionary archbishop to the pagans. Killed with his companions in 1009 near the frontier of Rus'.
Bishop of Arles for forty years. Plain-spoken preacher, author of a Rule for nuns, presided at the Council of Orange.
Forest hermit given land by King Childebert I. His monastery of Anisole grew into the town of Saint-Calais.
Salesian missionary priest. Shot in 1930 beside Bishop Versiglia for shielding the girls in their boat from pirates.
Abbot of Aghaboe and friend of Columba, he preached in Ireland and Scotland. Kilkenny is named after his church.
King of Denmark, 1080 to 1086. Cut down by rebels in St. Alban's church at Odense. Canonized 1101.
Fifth-century virgin of Albi who lived as a nun at Viants, near Gaillac in Languedoc.
Sixteen Carmelites of Compiègne guillotined in Paris on 17 July 1794, chanting the Veni Creator. Canonized 2024.
Mochuda. Abbot of Rahan until driven out in 637, then founder of the great monastery of Lismore.
Lawyer turned monk and bishop of Apt. At his request John Cassian wrote the Institutes on the monks of Egypt.
Daughter of Charity who saw Our Lady at the Rue du Bac in 1830 and gave the world the Miraculous Medal.
Archbishop of Armagh and reformer. Primate under the Synod of Ráth Breasail, 1111. Named Malachy his successor.
Lindisfarne monk, bishop of the East Saxons, founder of Lastingham. Brother of Chad. Died of plague in 664.
Carthaginian martyr, grandmother of the confessor Celerinus, praised by St. Cyprian in his letters.
Boy martyr beheaded at Milan with St. Nazarius. St. Ambrose found their bodies there late in his life.
Monk from Spoleto who settled as a hermit near Saulges in Maine with his brother, St. Céneri.
Fifth-century bishop venerated at Simorre in Gascony, where his relics were enshrined.
Bishop of Paris in the early 7th century. Attended the Council of Paris in 614 and collected the acts of the martyrs.
Pupil of Aidan, brother of Cedd, bishop of the Mercians at Lichfield. Walked his diocese. Died of plague in 672.
Cavalry officer turned Trappist, then hermit priest among the Tuareg of the Sahara. Killed at Tamanrasset in 1916.
Martyr of Lycia under Decius, by tradition. Legend has him carry the Christ Child across a river. Patron of travelers.
Armenian missionary to Flanders, by tradition. Beheaded by Roman soldiers and venerated at Comines.
Founder of Clonmacnoise on the Shannon. One of the Twelve Apostles of Ireland. Died young, soon after the founding.
Monk of the abbey of Lézat, honored in the Diocese of Pamiers under the names Cibar and Ybars.
Fourth-century martyr honored in Gascony, in the proper calendar of the Archdiocese of Auch.
Kent-born hermit priest in Normandy. By tradition beheaded c. 884 in the Vexin, at today's Saint-Clair-sur-Epte.
Baker's apprentice turned Redemptorist. Tireless apostle of Warsaw and Vienna. Patron of Vienna.
Disciple of Cyril and Methodius. Founded the Ohrid Literary School and taught Slavonic letters to some 3,500 pupils.
Grandson of Clovis who escaped his uncles' swords and chose the priesthood. Saint-Cloud near Paris bears his name.
Burgundian princess and Queen of the Franks. Won her husband Clovis to baptism. Ended her days a widow at Tours.
Court poet in Munster who became a monk, one of the first Irish vernacular poets. Founder and patron of Cloyne.
6th-century founder of the monastery of Dromore. Principal patron of the Diocese of Dromore.
Hermit of the Burren who founded Kilmacduagh with his kinsman King Guaire and reluctantly became its abbot-bishop.
Donegal-born abbot who sailed to Iona in 563, made it a beacon of the faith, and preached Christ to the Picts.
Founder and abbot of the influential abbey of Bangor in County Down. St Columbanus trained there under him.
Hermit and metalworker on the Liffey who became the first bishop of Kildare in the time of St Brigid. Died 519.
Bishop of Constance from 934, builder of churches and three times a pilgrim to Jerusalem. Canonized in 1123.
Capuchin lay brother who kept the door of the Altötting friary for 41 years, serving pilgrims and the poor.
Monk of Micy who became a hermit in Maine with St Fraimbault; ordained a priest for mission work, buried at Javron.
Fifth-century bishop of Gap in the Alps of Gaul, named as a holy confessor in the Roman Martyrology on 12 April.
Frankish hermit who became first bishop of Freising. His legendary pack-bear is on Pope Benedict XVI's coat of arms.
Wealthy matron of Thagora, beheaded at Theveste in 304 for refusing to sacrifice. Augustine praised her often.
Holy Roman Empress, wife of St Henry II. Widowed in 1024, she became a nun at Kaufungen, the convent she founded.
Shepherd boy turned monk, hermit of Inner Farne and Bishop of Lindisfarne. Northumbria's beloved wonder-worker.
Bishop of Rodez for over 50 years. Gregory of Tours says he kept rebuilding his church and left it unfinished.
Belgian priest who gave 16 years to the leprosy settlement on Molokai, Hawaii, and died of the disease in 1889.
Welsh Jesuit called Tad y Tlodion, Father of the Poor. Hanged at Usk in 1679 during the Popish Plot panic.
Monk-bishop of Mynyw and patron of Wales. Dying, he bade his monks be joyful, keep the faith and do the little things.
Irish virgin of Tydavnet on Sliabh Beagh, Co. Monaghan. Her crozier, once used as a lie detector, is in Dublin.
Apostle of the Déisi and founder of Ardmore in Co. Waterford; his Life claims he preached in Munster before Patrick.
Sixth-century founder and first bishop of Bangor in Gwynedd. Its cathedral is said to stand on his monastery's site.
Martyr of Thessaloniki, pierced with lances under Maximian c. 306. Patron of his city, honored East and West.
Bishop of Carthage who sold the church's sacred vessels to ransom captives the Vandals brought from Rome in 455.
Corsican virgin martyred under Diocletian. Her legend says a dove guided the boat bearing her body to Monaco.
Dagobert I's treasurer, then bishop of Cahors from 630. Built churches, walls and an aqueduct; his letters survive.
Member of the Areopagus converted by Paul's sermon in Athens (Acts 17:34). Tradition makes him first bishop of Athens.
Crucified beside Christ, he asked to be remembered and heard: "This day thou shalt be with me in paradise." (Lk 23:43)
Came from Roman Africa to Gaul with Sts Marcellinus and Vincent; first bishop of Digne in Provence. Died 379.
Priest who lived for many years as a hermit near Sisteron in Provence and died famed for miracles.
Disciple of St Germain of Paris. Abbot at Autun, then first abbot of St Vincent's, the later Saint-Germain-des-Prés.
Franciscan sister of Salvador, Bahia, who nursed the sick poor in her convent's chicken yard; it grew into a hospital.
Abbot of Glastonbury, then Archbishop of Canterbury. Monastic reformer, metalworker and musician.
Evangelist of Ergyng on the Welsh border; died on Bardsey Island c. 550. Legend says he crowned King Arthur.
Oxford star turned Jesuit. Slipped into England in 1580, wrote his "Brag", and was hanged at Tyburn in 1581.
Oxford master, then Archbishop of Canterbury from 1234. Stood up to Henry III; died in France in 1240.
Last king of the House of Wessex. Built Westminster Abbey, consecrated days before his death in 1066.
Abbot of Novalesa, below the Mont Cenis pass, from about 820. Patron of Novalesa, of farmers and of monks.
Counted the first bishop of Tournai, in Frankish Gaul; friend of St Medard. A later Life makes him a martyr.
Goldsmith and mint master to Frankish kings, then bishop of Noyon-Tournai and missionary to pagan Flanders.
Prophet of Israel. Fed by ravens, he called down fire on Carmel against Baal and was taken up in a fiery chariot.
New York widow, mother of five and convert. Founded the Sisters of Charity at Emmitsburg; first US-born saint.
French noblewoman who founded the Daughters of the Cross with St Andrew Fournet to teach and nurse the poor.
Swedish nurse in New York turned Catholic; founded the Bridgettine Sisters in Rome and hid Jews there in WWII.
Son and heir of St Stephen of Hungary, remembered for his purity. Killed by a boar while hunting in 1031.
Opened a school for poor girls at Villefranche-de-Rouergue and founded the Sisters of the Holy Family there.
Gaillac heiress who founded the Sisters of St Joseph of the Apparition; schools and hospitals from Algeria to Lebanon.
Ulster warrior turned monk at his sister Fanchea's urging; founded Killeany on Inishmore, Aran, c. 484.
Legendary Merovingian princess, said to be healed of leprosy at the Burle spring in Gévaudan and to found a convent.
First bishop of Ardstraw in Tyrone, c. 581. Patron of the Diocese of Derry, whose cathedral bears his name.
Young Christian of Lyon, betrayed with his friend Alexander after the persecution of 177 and beheaded.
Monk of Fontenelle under St Wandrille, made bishop of Toulouse c. 656; later returned to his abbey to die.
King of Sweden, cut down at Uppsala after Mass on Ascension Day 1160. Patron of Sweden; his head is on Stockholm's arms.
Bishop of London from 675. Founded Chertsey Abbey, and Barking Abbey for his sister Ethelburga.
Twice-married queen who stayed a virgin, then founded the abbey at Ely. Her body was found incorrupt.
First Bishop of Trier. Legend made him a disciple of St. Peter; his tomb lies in the crypt of St. Matthias' Abbey.
Senator turned monk at Lérins with his family, then Bishop of Lyon. Wrote In Praise of the Desert.
Founded the Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate in 1816 to preach to the poor. Bishop of Marseille.
Niece of St. Odile and her successor as Abbess of Hohenburg on Mont Sainte-Odile in Alsace.
Bishop of Carthage under the Arian Vandal kings. Exiled with his clergy for the Catholic faith; died in Gaul.
Twelve-year-old martyr of Mérida under Diocletian. Prudentius sang of the dove that flew from her mouth.
Priest who wrote the record of the martyrs of Córdoba. Archbishop-elect of Toledo; beheaded in 859.
Deacon of Tarragona. Burned alive in the amphitheatre in 259 with Bishop Fructuosus and the deacon Augurius.
Frankish Duke of Friuli, son-in-law of Louis the Pious. A lettered layman with a great library; founded Cysoing abbey.
Abbot of Saint-Fuscien from the Beauvaisis who founded the abbey of Saint-Lucien over the martyr's tomb at Beauvais.
Bishop of Toulouse praised by Jerome. Sold the altar vessels for the poor; Pope Innocent I sent him the biblical canon.
Archbishop of Nidaros, 1161 to 1188. Performed Norway's first royal coronation; likely author of the Passio Olavi.
Augustinian Recollect missionary in the Philippines, then Bishop of Pasto in Colombia. Died of cancer in 1906.
Sixth-century founder of the monastery at Kilfenora in the Burren, County Clare, and patron of its diocese.
Founder of Ros Ailithir, now Rosscarbery, whose School of Ross flourished for three centuries. Patron of Ross.
Young virgin of Agen martyred on a red-hot brazier. Her golden reliquary at Conques drew medieval pilgrims.
King of Castile and León. Took Córdoba, Jaén and Seville from the Moors and began Burgos Cathedral.
Bishop of Uzès, nephew of St. Firminus. Wrote a monastic Rule that counted copying books as the monks' manual labor.
Irish hermit at Breuil near Meaux who dug a garden and kept a hospice for travelers. Paris cabs took his name.
Hermit of Gougane Barra who founded a monastery above the River Lee that grew into the city of Cork.
Founder of the school of Clonard, teacher of the Twelve Apostles of Ireland. Died of plague in 549.
Abbot of Clonenagh, called Father of the Irish Monks. His house kept no cows; he lived on barley bread and water.
By tradition a native of Pamplona and first Bishop of Amiens, beheaded there. Pamplona fetes him at San Fermín.
Early Bishop of Mende in the Gévaudan, honored each January with all the holy bishops of that see.
Bishop of Uzès from 538. Sat at councils of Orléans and Paris; uncle and mentor of St. Ferreolus, his successor.
Benedict and John, monks from Italy, with Poles Isaac, Matthew and Christian. Hermits killed by robbers in 1003.
First Bishop of Killaloe, consecrated in Rome. A great preacher; the Flannan Isles bear his name.
Hospitaller nun at Beaulieu in Quercy, rapt in ecstasy at Communion. Over a hundred miracles were credited to her.
One of the first bishops of Cahors, at the turn of the 5th century. Honored with all the holy bishops of that see.
Hermit ordained by St. Martin of Tours, by tradition. Founded the monastery of Mont-Glonne on the Loire.
Bishop of Strasbourg in the 7th century. Founded the abbey of Haslach and the house of St. Thomas in Strasbourg.
Roman officer in Noricum who confessed Christ under Diocletian. Drowned in the Enns with a stone tied to his neck.
Young martyr of about 296, honored in the Diocese of Coutances. The Cotentin village of Saint-Floxel bears his name.
Legendary first Bishop of Lodève and apostle of upper Auvergne. The town of Saint-Flour grew up around his tomb.
Bishop of Thérouanne from 816, a grandson of Charles Martel. Died on visitation at Esquelbecq in 855.
Auvergnat noble who left the Frankish court for the hermit life. Founded monastic cells in Maine; relics at Senlis.
Founded the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart. Served Italian immigrants in America; first US citizen saint.
Duke of Gandía who gave up his titles after his wife died to become a Jesuit. Third Superior General of the Society.
Dominican from Écija, missionary in Fujian. Imprisoned, tortured and strangled for the faith in 1748.
Spanish Dominican, protomartyr of China. Beheaded at Fu'an in Fujian in 1648.
Italian Franciscan, coadjutor bishop in Shanxi. Killed at Taiyuan with Bishop Grassi in the Boxer massacre of 1900.
Franciscan missionary of Tucumán and Peru, famed for preaching and his violin. Died at Lima in 1610.
Shepherd boy of Fátima who saw Our Lady in 1917 but never heard her. Longed to console Jesus; died of flu at ten.
First Bishop of Quebec. Founded the Séminaire de Québec in 1663 and fought the brandy trade with Indigenous peoples.
Gévaudan bishop under Louis the Pious who fought pagan rites at Lake Saint-Andéol. By legend, slain by his nephew.
Irish missionary to the Alemanni who founded Säckingen Abbey on the Rhine. He strides across the banner of Glarus.
Frankish warrior of legend who fell fighting the Saracens near Bassoues in Gascony. A basilica stands over his tomb.
Bishop of Coutances from 677. Founded the monasteries of Saint-Fromond and Le Ham in Normandy.
Visigothic noble turned hermit and founder of monasteries like Compludo. Bishop of Dumio, then of Braga.
Bishop of Tarragona. Burned alive in the amphitheatre in 259 under Valerian, with his deacons Augurius and Eulogius.
Bishop of Ruspe in Vandal Africa. Exiled to Sardinia by an Arian king; wrote against Arianism in Augustine's line.
Irish monk famed for visions of the afterlife. Founded monasteries in East Anglia and at Lagny; buried at Péronne.
French MEP missionary, Vicar Apostolic of Sichuan. Beheaded at Chengdu in 1815; one of the 120 Martyrs of China.
Bishop of Lescar at the Council of Agde in 506. Tradition says Visigoths put him to death at Mimizan.
Companion of Columbanus who stayed in Alemannia as a hermit. The Abbey of St. Gall grew up on his cell.
Breton-born Bishop of Évreux for some 40 years. Retired as a hermit near Mont-Saint-Michel Bay; buried at Saint-Pair.
Ninth-century peasant farmer of the Carcassès. Patron of Roussillon and long the patron of Catalan farmers.
Bishop of Cambrai-Arras. Ransomed captives, founded churches; by tradition built a chapel on a Senne island at Brussels.
Monk who founded Montsalvy in Auvergne on land given by the Viscount of Carlat, building a monastery and a hospice.
Son of the Count of Bregenz, Bishop of Constance from 979. Founded Petershausen Abbey in 983 and cared for the poor.
Pope 492-496. His letter Duo sunt told Emperor Anastasius the world is ruled by two powers: priestly and royal.
Consecrated virgin of Paris. As Attila's Huns neared in 451 she urged the city to pray, not flee. Patroness of Paris.
Hermit of Lectoure in Gascony and the town's patron. In his legend, soldiers sent to seize him were converted instead.
Second Abbot of Savigny, 1122-1139. Under him the Norman abbey founded daughter houses such as Furness in England.
Monk of Conques who helped organise the new abbey of Vabres, then became Bishop of Lodève in the 9th century.
Maltese priest who founded the Society of Christian Doctrine (MUSEUM) to train lay catechists. Malta's first saint.
Count of Aurillac who lived as a devout layman and founded an abbey. Odo of Cluny wrote his Life as a model.
Monk of Moissac and choirmaster at Toledo, then Archbishop of Braga from c. 1100. Fought lay control of church offices.
Venetian monk, tutor of St Emeric and first Bishop of Csanád. Killed at Buda in 1046 during a pagan uprising.
Abbot at Autun, then Bishop of Paris from 555. Known as Father of the Poor; excommunicated King Charibert.
Sickly shepherdess of Pibrac, shunned by her stepmother. Went daily to Mass, shared her bread with the poor. Died at 22.
Roman official turned Bishop of Auxerre. Went to Britain c. 429 to confront Pelagianism and led the Alleluia victory.
Germanus the Scot, 5th-century missionary bishop. Legend says he crossed to Normandy on a wheel and slew a dragon.
Courtier of Dagobert I who became a monk and founded the abbey of Saint-Germer-de-Fly near Beauvais.
Merovingian Bishop of Toulouse, said to hail from Angoulême. Founded a monastery near Muret; patron of Lézat abbey.
Daughter of Pepin of Landen. Founded Nivelles Abbey with her mother Itta and ruled it as abbess; invoked against rats.
Hermit-abbot of Saint-Gilles. Legend says an arrow meant for his hind struck him. One of the Fourteen Holy Helpers.
Bishop of Carcassonne in the early 10th century. Viollet-le-Duc's church of Saint-Gimer in the city is named for him.
Companion of St Sever sent to evangelise Novempopulania. Tradition says he was martyred near Hagetmau.
Prince of Murom, son of Vladimir the Great. Murdered in 1015 amid the succession war; a passion-bearer with Boris.
Saint of Ballyvourney, Co. Cork, linked with bees. Tradition says she set a swarm on a thief to win back stolen cattle.
Noble maiden who received St. Eligius's ring as a bride of Christ. Led a convent at Noyon; patroness of the town.
Moravian disciple of Methodius and his chosen successor in 885. One of the Seven Apostles of Bulgaria.
Reforming Abbot of Niederaltaich, then Bishop of Hildesheim from 1022. Built schools and some 30 churches.
First Bishop of Oloron, at the Council of Agde in 506. Born at Lichos; tradition says he died at Jaca.
Italian Franciscan, Vicar Apostolic of North Shanxi. Killed at Taiyuan in 1900 in the Boxer uprising.
12th-century novice of Savigny Abbey in Normandy, honored locally with Vitalis and Geoffrey among Savigny's saints.
Franciscan lay brother from Vasai, India. Crucified at Nagasaki in 1597, one of the 26 Martyrs of Japan.
Queen Jadwiga, crowned King of Poland in 1384. Wed Jogaila of Lithuania; her jewels helped refound Kraków's university.
Empress, mother of Constantine the Great. Went on pilgrimage to the Holy Land; tradition says she found the True Cross.
Hermit from Tongeren who lived on a rock off Jersey. Beheaded by raiders; patron of Jersey and its capital, St Helier.
Carinthian countess who lost husband and sons, gave her wealth to the poor, and founded Gurk Abbey in 1043.
English-born bishop, venerated as the apostle of Finland. Legend says the peasant Lalli killed him at Lake Köyliö.
Premonstratensian canon of Steinfeld and Marian mystic. As a boy offered an apple to the Christ Child; mended clocks.
Visigothic prince who left Arianism for the Catholic faith and rose against his father Liuvigild. Executed in 585.
Bishop of Toulouse c. 350. Sought out the tomb of the martyr Saturninus and raised a small chapel over it.
Venerated as the first Bishop of Carcassonne, 6th century. The abbey of Saint-Hilaire in the Aude rose over his chapel.
6th-century bishop of the Gévaudan who lived as a hermit above Mende. Took part in the Council of Clermont in 535.
Founding abbess of Whitby, host of the Synod of 664. Kings sought her counsel; all who knew her called her mother.
The holy abbots of Saint-Germer-de-Fly, the Beauvaisis abbey founded by St. Germer, honored together with him.

saints.n: The Holy Bishops of Le Mans
saints.bio: The saintly bishops of Le Mans, from St. Julian onward, honored together on one feast in the Diocese of Laval.

saints.n: The Holy Martyrs and Blesseds of China
saints.bio: 120 saints, Chinese faithful and missionaries, martyred 1648 to 1930 and canonized in 2000, with the blesseds of China.
Founded the island monastery of Lérins, a nursery of bishops and saints, then became Archbishop of Arles.
Recluse in a ruined tower on Cap Ferrat near Nice who foretold a Lombard raid. Gregory of Tours recorded his life.
Bishop of Maastricht who moved St. Lambert's relics to Liège. Apostle of the Ardennes; in legend, the stag and cross.
Burgundian Carthusian, prior of Witham, then Bishop of Lincoln. Rebuilt his cathedral, stood up to kings, kept a swan.
Polish Dominican, Apostle of the North. Legend: he fled Kyiv bearing the Blessed Sacrament and a statue of Mary.
Archbishop of Toledo who wrote on Mary's perpetual virginity. Tradition says she vested him in a chasuble.
Illtud the Knight, soldier turned abbot. His school at Llantwit Major in Glamorgan formed Samson, Gildas and David.
Third-century martyr of the Gévaudan. Tradition says he lived as a hermit by the Allier and was killed by pagans.
Great Martyr venerated in Greece. Legend: born Penelope, shut in a tower by her pagan father, baptized by St. Timothy.
Abbess of Oeren at Trier who gave St. Willibrord the lands to found his monastery at Echternach in 697 or 698.
Farm laborer of Madrid who never missed morning Mass. Legend says angels ploughed his field while he prayed.
Foster mother of the saints of Ireland. Founded a community at Killeedy, Limerick; St. Brendan was in her care as a boy.
Bishop of Chartres and great canonist of the Investiture Crisis. The Decretum and Panormia are attributed to him.
Breton priest and church judge who pleaded for orphans, widows and the poor and refused bribes. Patron of lawyers.
Youngest seer of Fátima. Offered her sufferings for sinners and died in Lisbon at nine. Canonized in 2017.
French Jesuit in Madagascar. Told he would be spared if he gave up his faith, he refused; rebels shot him in 1896.
Deacon martyred at Lambaesis in Numidia under Valerian, with the lector Marian, after visions in prison.
Founder of the monastic school of Tuam, patron of its archdiocese. Tradition names St. Brendan among his pupils.
Paris Foreign Missions priest from near Lyon, beheaded in Tonkin in 1852. One of the Vietnamese Martyrs.
Paris Foreign Missions priest from near Lyon, sent to Guizhou. Seized with three converts, beheaded at Kaizhou in 1862.
Paris Foreign Missions priest kept in a cage, then beheaded in Hanoi in 1861. His letters moved St. Thérèse.
Saumur shopkeeper who turned to the poor and founded the Congregation of St. Anne of Providence. Canonized 1982.
Founded the Sisters of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception of Castres in 1836, for the poor, the sick and prisoners.
Breton who gave her own bed to a blind, paralysed old woman in 1839, and so began the Little Sisters of the Poor.
Chinese catechist, tortured and exiled to Tartary for nearly 20 years, then arrested again and strangled in 1839.
The Maid of Orléans. Heard heavenly voices, lifted the siege, saw her king crowned, burned at Rouen at about 19.
Daughter of Louis XI, briefly queen until Louis XII had their marriage annulled. Founded the Annonciades at Bourges.
Barcelona noblewoman, widow and mother of nine, who founded the Carmelite Sisters of Charity at Vic in 1826.
Flemish Jesuit scholastic who died in Rome at 22, holy in ordinary duties. Patron of altar servers.
Monk who learned from the desert fathers of Egypt and carried their wisdom to Gaul. Founded St. Victor's at Marseille.
Lisbon noble turned Jesuit in the Madurai mission, living as a Tamil sannyasi. Beheaded at Oriyur in 1693.
Spanish Jesuit in the Guaraní missions. Killed at Ijuí in 1628, two days after Sts. Roch González and Alonso Rodríguez.
Jesuit mission preacher of the Vivarais and Velay hills, champion of at-risk women and orphans. Patron of lacemakers.
Vincentian missionary in Hubei, China, arrested in 1839 and strangled on a cross at Wuchang in 1840.
Welsh Franciscan from Clynnog Fawr, executed at Southwark in 1598. One of the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.
Welsh secular priest who served Catholics in hiding for 24 years. Executed near Cardiff in 1679 with St. Philip Evans.
Shepherd from Extremadura turned Dominican lay brother in Lima. Porter of his priory; friend of St. Martin de Porres.
Bohemian Redemptorist, fourth bishop of Philadelphia. Founded the first Catholic diocesan school system in the US.
Vicar general of Prague, thrown into the Vltava by King Wenceslaus IV in 1393. Martyr of the seal of confession.
Franciscan preacher of Lviv who kept preaching after going blind. One of the patron saints of Poland and Lithuania.
Ligurian Franciscan, missionary in China from 1799. Arrested in Hunan and strangled at Changsha in 1816.
Calvinist-born Scot turned Jesuit. Hanged at Glasgow Cross in 1615, he threw his rosary into the crowd.
Welsh Benedictine from Trawsfynydd, first prior of St. Gregory's at Douai. Hanged at Tyburn in 1610.
Moravian priest racked in Olomouc to make him reveal a confession. He kept the seal and died of his torments in 1620.
Lancashire priest who served London's plague victims. Hanged at Tyburn in 1654; his body lies in Westminster Cathedral.

saints.n: St. José María de Yermo y Parres
saints.bio: Mexican priest who founded the Servants of the Sacred Heart of Jesus and of the Poor, opening shelters and orphanages.
Aragonese priest who founded Opus Dei in 1928 to spread holiness in ordinary work and daily life. Author of The Way.
Dogmatics professor at Lviv who became its Latin-rite Archbishop in 1900 and shepherded the city until his death.
Canary-born Jesuit, Apostle of Brazil: helped found São Paulo in 1554 and wrote a grammar of the Tupi language.
Ladin priest from South Tyrol, among the first Divine Word missionaries to China, where he served from 1879 to 1908.
Theology professor, then Bishop of Przemyśl from 1900; co-founded the Sister Servants of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus.
Goan Oratorian who slipped into Dutch Ceylon in 1687 and secretly rebuilt its outlawed Church. Apostle of Sri Lanka.
Sichuan priest, won to the faith by the preaching of St. Gabriel-Taurin Dufresse; strangled at Chengdu in 1817.
Guizhou silk-maker turned zealous catechist. Condemned for spreading an 'evil cult'; strangled on a cross in 1815.
Companion of the girl martyr Eulalia at Mérida; the Martyrology says she alone clung to her as she went to suffer.
Martyr under Diocletian, honored with his wife Basilissa, with whom he kept virginity; tortured and then beheaded.
Companion of St. Lucian, first Bishop of Beauvais; slain by the sword with Maximian in the Roman persecution.
Venerated as the first Bishop of Le Mans and apostle of the Maine; the city's cathedral bears his name.
Patron of Lescar, honored by tradition as the first bishop of Béarn, sent there to preach by Leontius of Trier.
Prioress of Mont-Cornillon whose visions led to the feast of Corpus Christi, first kept at Liège in 1246.
Picard woman paralyzed for some 22 years, healed in 1804, who founded the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur.
Romano-British martyr of Caerleon, named with Aaron by Gildas and Bede among Britain's first martyrs after Alban.
Mallorcan Franciscan, Apostle of California, who founded its first missions, beginning at San Diego in 1769.
Priest venerated in the Diocese of Tarbes and Lourdes as the first evangelizer of Bigorre, in the 4th century.
Schoolboy of Complutum who, with his younger brother Pastor, threw down his slate to confess Christ; slain in 304.
Bishop of Lyon at the Council of Aquileia (381) who quit his see to live as a monk in Egypt's desert of Scetis.
Mohawk-Algonquin convert baptized in 1676; at Kahnawake she vowed her virginity to Christ. Lily of the Mohawks.
Philadelphia heiress who spent her fortune founding the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament and Xavier University.
Apostle of Strathclyde, called Mungo, founder of Glasgow's church. The bird, tree, bell and fish of its arms recall him.
Hermit who founded the monastery of Glendalough in Wicklow; legend says a blackbird nested in his outstretched hand.
Held to be the first saint born in Ireland; hermit-founder of Saighir and first Bishop of Ossory. Patron of Ossory.
Irish bishop who evangelized Franconia; murdered at Würzburg about 689 with Colman and Totnan. Apostle of Franconia.
Hungarian princess, wife of Bolesław the Chaste; widowed, she became a Poor Clare at Stary Sącz. Patron of salt miners.
Syro-Malabar priest who co-founded the CMI Carmelites at Mannanam and set up St. Joseph's Press there in 1846.
Knight-king of Hungary (1077–1095), lawgiver and hero of legend, who had St. Stephen canonized. Canonized in 1192.
Bishop of Maastricht slain at Liège about 705; pilgrims flocked to his shrine, and the see later moved to Liège.
Bishop of Paris from 650 who sold church vessels to feed the starving; credited with founding the Hôtel-Dieu.
Abbot of Old Leighlin, ordained in Rome, who championed the Roman reckoning of Easter in Ireland. Also called Molaise.
Bishop of Coutances from about 525; the Norman town of Saint-Lô bears his name. Patron of the Diocese of Coutances.
Gregorian missionary who succeeded Augustine at Canterbury. Bede: St. Peter scourged him in a dream to keep him there.
Abbot of Glendalough, then Archbishop of Dublin from 1162; peacemaker in the Norman invasion. Died at Eu in 1180.
Guizhou catechist, one of the Martyrs of Maokou: beheaded on 28 January 1858 with Jerome Lu Tingmei and Agatha Lin.
Guizhou-born laborer and convert, beheaded at Xilin in Guangxi in 1856, the year St. Auguste Chapdelaine was martyred.
Bishop of Seville, elder brother of Isidore, who led the Visigoths from Arianism at the Third Council of Toledo in 589.
Early Irish virgin venerated in the Diocese of Limerick, where local tradition links her with Killeely.
Jesuit from Lorraine in China, killed by Boxers on 20 July 1900 at Zhujiahe, Hebei, with the faithful in his church.
Alsatian Bishop of Toul turned pope (1049–1054) who crossed Europe holding synods against simony and clerical vice.
Wimborne nun called to Germany by her kinsman St. Boniface; abbess of Tauberbischofsheim, laid to rest near his tomb.
Bishop of Autun who defied the palace mayor Ebroin; blinded, his tongue cut out, and finally beheaded in 679.
By tradition a native of Carentan in Normandy who became missionary bishop to the Basques and was beheaded near Bayonne.
Patron and traditional first bishop of Bayonne, apostle of the Basques; legend says a spring rose where he was beheaded.
Frankish noble, disciple of St. Remigius, who became a hermit at Noblac near Limoges. Famed for freeing captives.
Bishop of Fréjus who ordained Honoratus, founder of Lérins; John Cassian dedicated Conferences to him.
Margrave of Austria (1095–1136) who founded Klosterneuburg and Heiligenkreuz and declined the German crown in 1125.
Tiny Capuchin from Herceg Novi who spent decades hearing confessions in Padua and offered his life for Christian unity.
Bishop of Auch in Gascony in the early eighth century; he died in 718.
Frankish noble at the court of Chlothar I, made count of Angers by Chilperic I, then its bishop from about 600.
Bishop of Couserans at the Council of Agde in 506, credited with many healings. Saint-Lizier is named for him.
Bishop of Pomaria, the Roman town on the site of Tlemcen. Honored in North Africa with Sts. Eugenius and Vindemialis.
Valencian Dominican and novice master who preached in New Granada from 1562 to 1569. Patron of Colombia.
Angevin prince of Naples who renounced the throne, became a Franciscan and Bishop of Toulouse, and died at 23.
Widow who co-founded the Daughters of Charity with St. Vincent de Paul to serve the poor and the sick.
Abbot of Saint-Privat in the Gévaudan. Cleared before Queen Brunhild, then slain by Count Innocentius's men in 584.
Apostle of Beauvais, martyred with Maximian and Julian. Later tradition named him the first bishop of the city.
Missionary of Raetia venerated at Chur. Medieval legend made him a British king; the Luzisteig pass bears his name.
Sichuan catechist, vowed to virginity at 12, who taught women for the missions. Beheaded in Guizhou in 1862.
Pilgrim, said to be a Scottish duke's son, who built a hospice, went to Jerusalem, and died in Alsace.
Frisian missionary among the Saxons, founder of Werden Abbey and first Bishop of Münster. Called the Apostle of Saxony.
Duchess of Bohemia who raised her grandson St. Wenceslaus in the faith. Strangled at Tetín in 921.
Piedmontese priest who founded the Sons of Divine Providence and the Little Missionary Sisters of Charity for the poor.
Tradition makes him an early bishop of Eauze, martyred under Decius. The old cathedral of Eauze is dedicated to him.
Seller of purple from Thyatira, baptized with her household at Philippi: the first recorded convert in Europe (Acts 16).
Founder and first bishop-abbot of Connor in County Antrim. Tradition says St. Patrick baptized him.
Companion of St. Patrick, who called him his strong man, and first Bishop of Clogher.
Founded the Society of the Sacred Heart in 1800 and led it until her death, spreading its schools for girls.
Founder and abbot-bishop of Tallaght, a leading figure of the Céli Dé reform. Óengus the Culdee was of his community.
Cousin of St. Samson, briefly bishop at Dol, then abbot of 62 monks on Sark. His relics were later taken to Paris.
Earl of Orkney killed by an axe blow on Egilsay at his cousin Haakon's order, after praying for his killers.
Evangelizer of the Lombez area in Gascony, who died about 610. A chapel above Lombez marks his supposed hermitage.
Archbishop of Armagh and reformer of the Irish Church. Died at Clairvaux in 1148; his friend St. Bernard wrote his Life.
Marist priest who founded the Marist Brothers in 1817 to give a Christian education to poor country children.
Tribune who chaired the Conference of Carthage in 411. Augustine dedicated the first books of The City of God to him.
African-born first Bishop of Embrun who, with Vincent and Domninus, brought many in the Maritime Alps to the faith.
Fifth-century Bishop of Paris known for miracles; legend says he subdued a dragon. Buried at Saint-Marcel.
Centurion who threw down his soldier's belt at an imperial birthday feast to serve Christ alone. Beheaded at Tangier.
Virgin of Mauretania who struck down a statue of Diana at Caesarea and was thrown to the beasts in the arena.
Abbot in the Cotentin, died 558. His relics at Corbeny were linked to the French kings' royal touch for scrofula.
The Pearl of York. Butcher's wife who hid priests in her home and was pressed to death in 1586 after refusing to plead.
Virgin martyr whose legend has her swallowed by a dragon and bursting free unharmed. One of the Fourteen Holy Helpers.
Daughter of King Béla IV, given to God by her parents. Dominican nun on the Danube island now called Margaret Island.
Smuggled a rope to Fr. William Watson to escape Bridewell prison. Refused to conform; hanged at Tyburn in 1588.
Reached Ville-Marie in 1653, opened Montreal's first school in 1658 and founded the Congregation of Notre-Dame.
Widowed mother who founded the Grey Nuns of Montreal to care for the poor. The first Canadian-born saint.
Mother Lupita. Co-founded the Handmaids of St. Margaret Mary and the Poor; hid priests in time of persecution.

saints.n: St. María Micaela of the Blessed Sacrament
saints.bio: Madrid noblewoman who founded the Handmaids of the Blessed Sacrament to shelter women at risk. Died of cholera.
Reader who had confessed Christ under Decius. Arrested again, he was beheaded at Lambaesis with the deacon James.

saints.n: St. Mariana of Jesus de Paredes
saints.bio: The Lily of Quito. Lived in prayer and penance at home and offered her life for her city amid the disasters of 1645.
German-born Franciscan of Syracuse, New York, who spent 30 years caring for leprosy patients at Kalaupapa, Molokai.
Founded the Religious of the Assumption in Paris in 1839, devoted to educating girls in the faith.
Founded the Little Sisters of the Holy Family in 1880 to serve priests and colleges in Quebec. Canonized in 2024.
Barfleur teacher who hid priests in the Revolution, then founded the Sisters of the Christian Schools of Mercy.
Saw two brothers executed at Lyon in 1794 and, at their plea, forgave. Founded the Religious of Jesus and Mary in 1818.
Croatian priest and canon, tortured and beheaded at Košice in 1619 with two Jesuits after refusing to turn Calvinist.
Priest-hermit of Cyrrhus who lived in the open air on a mountain. Father of the movement behind the Maronite Church.
Virgin venerated in the Archdiocese of Albi in southern France.
Pannonian monk turned Archbishop of Braga, Apostle of the Suevi. Wrote De correctione rusticorum against rural paganism.
Lay catechist of Guizhou, executed with Fr. Jean-Pierre Néel and two fellow catechists on 18 February 1862.
Founder and first superior general of the Sisters of the Good Shepherd at Angers, for girls and women in distress.
Stood by the cross of Jesus with His Mother and Mary Magdalene (John 19:25). One of the Three Marys of the tomb.
Galilean Melkite, the Carmelite Mary of Jesus Crucified: a mystic and stigmatic who helped found the Bethlehem Carmel.

saints.n: St. María Natividad Venegas de la Torre
saints.bio: Nurse and pharmacist in Guadalajara who founded the Daughters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus and kept a hospital running.
Marius, in legend a hermit by Mont Journal in the Cantal and disciple of St. Austremoine. Shrine at Saint-Mary-le-Cros.
Co-founded the Josephites with Fr. Julian Tenison Woods to teach the rural poor. First Australian saint.
Widow of Tours turned Ursuline who sailed to Quebec in 1639 and founded the first girls' school in New France.
Founded the Sisters of the Presentation of Mary in 1796 to teach poor children. Pius IX called her the Woman-Apostle.
Madrid foundress of the Servants of Mary, Ministers of the Sick, devoted to nursing the sick and the poor.
Syro-Malabar nun of Puthenchira, founder of the Congregation of the Holy Family. Said to have hidden the stigmata.
Polish Ursuline who opened convents in Russia and Scandinavia, then founded the Ursulines of the Agonizing Heart.
First known Bishop of Cologne, at the synods of Rome in 313 and Arles in 314. Legend made him a disciple of St. Peter.
Queen of Henry the Fowler and mother of Emperor Otto I. Founded convents at Quedlinburg, Enger and Nordhausen.
Commander of the Theban Legion, massacred with his comrades at Agaunum under Maximian for refusing to deny Christ.
Milanese priest who became Bishop of Angers from 423 to 453. Shown in art as a bishop with a fish holding a key.
Son of St. Rictrude, courtier turned monk. Built the abbey of Breuil on his Merville estate and was its first abbot.
St. Benedict's disciple who ran out on the water to save young Placid. Tradition sends him to Gaul to found Glanfeuil.
Abbot of Pannonhalma, then Bishop of Pécs from 1036. Wrote the Legend of the hermits Sts. Zoerard and Benedict.
Disciple of St. Lucian, Apostle of Beauvais. Slain by the sword with Julian, before Lucian himself was martyred.
Called up at 21, he refused military service because he was a Christian and was beheaded at Theveste.
Marius, Orléans-born monk who became abbot of Bodon in the diocese of Sisteron. The village of Saint-May keeps his name.
Bishop of Noyon, sheltered from rain by an eagle in legend. In France, rain on his feast foretells forty more wet days.
Abbot of St. Martin's at Autun who ended his days as a hermit in Paris, where the church of Saint-Merri bears his name.
Hermit slain in 861 by two thieves he had welcomed; legend says his ravens exposed them. Einsiedeln rose at his cell.
Nephew of St. Patrick, who made him Bishop of Ardagh. He received the religious profession of St. Brigid of Kildare.
Silesian Jesuit from Cieszyn, tortured and killed at Košice in 1619 with Sts. Stephen Pongrácz and Marko Krizin.
Gregorian missionary, first Bishop of London in 604, later Archbishop of Canterbury. Gregory wrote him on pagan temples.
Basque farmhand turned priest who founded the Priests of the Sacred Heart of Jesus of Bétharram. Foe of Jansenism.
De La Salle Brother of Cuenca, teacher, textbook author and linguist. Died in Spain. First male saint of Ecuador.
African-born Pope from 311 to 314, the age of the Edict of Milan. Received the Lateran and condemned the Donatists.
Fifth-century priest of Bigorre, honored in the Diocese of Tarbes and Lourdes.
Alsatian Jesuit missionary in China, killed by Boxers at Wuyi in 1900 with Fr. Rémi Isoré as they knelt in prayer.
Monk of Luxeuil and companion of St. Bertin, abbot at Sithiu, then Bishop of Noyon-Tournai after St. Eligius.
Veiled by St. Patrick, by tradition, she founded a community of virgins at Killeavy under Slieve Gullion in Armagh.
Cluniac monk of the priory of Altkirch, apostle of the Sundgau. Legend says one bunch of grapes fed him through Lent.
Mainchín, said to have founded the church of Limerick in the late 6th century. Patron saint of the city of Limerick.
Founding Bishop of Killala, placed there by St. Patrick in tradition. Died a hermit on Inishmurray off the Sligo coast.
Brother of the Christian Schools who spent 58 years at the college of Malonne in humble tasks and constant prayer.
In legend a soldier of Charlemagne turned hermit in Quercy, who dug rock pools for the flocks. Invoked against epilepsy.
Madrid-born nun who served the old and sick at Oruro, Bolivia, and there founded the Missionary Crusaders of the Church.
Martyr of Milan with the boy Celsus. St. Ambrose found his body, the blood still red, in a garden outside the city.
Numidian bishop beaten and sent to the mines under Valerian. St. Cyprian wrote to him there, and his reply survives.
Bishop of Lyon from 552, famous for his life and miracles. Kinsman of St. Gregory of Tours, who wrote his Life.
Farmer, soldier and judge who became the hermit Brother Klaus. His counsel at Stans in 1481 kept the Swiss from war.
Šibenik Franciscan who preached Christ to the qadi of Jerusalem and was killed with three friars. First Croatian saint.
Apostle of the Southern Picts. His church at Whithorn in Galloway was called Candida Casa, the White House.
Constable whose victory at Aljubarrota in 1385 saved Portugal's independence, later Carmelite Brother Nuno of St. Mary.
Born blind, healed at baptism in legend. Founded the abbey of Hohenburg, now Mont Sainte-Odile. Patroness of Alsace.
