Abbot of Cluny for half a century. Had his monasteries pray for all the faithful departed on 2 November: All Souls' Day.
Second Abbot of Cluny. Reformed Fleury, Aurillac and the Roman abbeys; wrote hymns and antiphons for St. Martin.
Viking turned Christian king who pressed the conversion of Norway. Fell at Stiklestad in 1030; Norway's eternal king.
Princess of Kiev, regent for her son Sviatoslav. Baptized Helena in the 950s; grandmother of St. Vladimir.
Archbishop of Armagh. Hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn in 1681, the last Catholic martyr to die in England.
Bishop of Milevis in Numidia. Answered the Donatist Parmenian with a defense of unity built on the Chair of Peter.
Bishop of Auch, sent by the Visigoth king as envoy to the Roman generals in 439. Likely poet of the Commonitorium.
Norman monk who founded a hermitage in the forest of Andaine and became abbot of Landelles. Famed for healings.
Irish monk who went with St. Columba to Iona and, by tradition, was the first buried there, in Reilig Odhráin.
Bishop of Bamberg and Apostle of Pomerania, which he won to the faith on two missions in 1124 and 1128.
Abbot honored in the Diocese of Cahors, who died between 484 and 510.
Physician of Nicomedia, beheaded under Maximian. Healer of the poor and one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers.
Priest and companion of St. Saturninus of Toulouse, martyr and apostle of the Lauragais. Saint-Papoul bears his name.
Shepherd turned Franciscan lay brother, rapt in adoration before the Eucharist. Patron of Eucharistic congresses.
Schoolboy who with his brother Justus threw down his slate to confess Christ. Martyred at Complutum, now Alcalá, in 304.
Monk of Poitou who lived as a hermit at Scissy with St. Scubilion, then Bishop of Avranches. Saint-Pair keeps his name.
Guizhou seminarian, one of the Martyrs of Qingyanzhen, killed on 29 July 1861 with Joseph Zhang Wenlan and two others.
Lille-born Jesuit missionary in China, killed at Zhujiahe in 1900 with Fr. Léon-Ignace Mangin and many Chinese faithful.
Sichuan priest who sold vegetables by day and said Mass in secret by night. Strangled at Chengdu in 1818.
First Bishop of Narbonne, one of seven bishops Gregory of Tours says were sent from Rome to evangelize Gaul c. 250.

saints.n: St. Paulina of the Agonizing Heart of Jesus
saints.bio: Trentino-born nun who founded the Little Sisters of the Immaculate Conception. Brazil's first saint, canonized 2002.
Bishop of Trier who refused to condemn Athanasius at Arles in 353. Exiled by Constantius II, he died in Phrygia.
Roman monk sent by Gregory the Great to England. First Bishop of York; he baptized King Edwin of Northumbria in 627.
Visayan teenage catechist killed on Guam in 1672 with the Jesuit Diego Luis de San Vitores. Canonized in 2012.
Sixth-century Bishop of Embrun, pupil of Bishop Catulinus and builder of churches. His relics rest at Camprodon.
Galician boy hostage in Córdoba. Refused to renounce Christ or yield to Caliph Abd al-Rahman III; killed at about 13.
Spanish Franciscan, envoy from Manila to Hideyoshi. Crucified at Nagasaki in 1597 with St. Paul Miki and companions.
Guizhou catechist, exiled to Mongolia, allowed home in 1827. Seized while visiting Christian prisoners; strangled, 1834.
Founded the Mercedarians at Barcelona to ransom Christian captives of the Moors, vowing to stay as hostages if need be.
Spanish Franciscan of fierce penance who founded a stricter reform of his order. Counselor of St. Teresa of Ávila.
Catalan Dominican and Vicar Apostolic of Fujian, consecrated a bishop in 1730. Beheaded at Fuzhou on 26 May 1747.
Doge of Venice who slipped away in 978 to become a Benedictine at Cuxa in the Pyrenees, ending his days as a hermit.
Innkeeper of Zunyi turned catechist who led hundreds to the faith. Strangled in 1814 for refusing to trample the cross.
Welsh Jesuit who ministered in South Wales from 1675. Hanged at Cardiff in 1679; honored as patron of tennis players.
Earl of Arundel, reconciled to the Church in 1584. Ten years a prisoner in the Tower of London; died there in 1595.
Franciscan from Mexico City, one of the 26 Martyrs crucified at Nagasaki in 1597. The first Mexican saint.
Bishop of Agen who wrote against the Arians in 357 and upheld the Nicene faith at the Council of Rimini in 359.
Priest from Benevento who preached the Gospel at Tournai, martyred under Maximian. His tomb is venerated at Seclin.
Missionary abbot, head of Reichenau from 724, founder of Murbach and Hornbach. His Scarapsus first gives today's Creed.
Abbot at Villeneuve-lès-Avignon, across the Rhône from Avignon, who died in 1087.
Martyred at Cemenelum, today Cimiez above Nice, under Valerian in 257. The abbey of Saint-Pons rose near the spot.
Bishop of Calama, Augustine's friend for nearly forty years. Present at his death, he wrote the first Life of Augustine.
First Bishop of Lyon. Aged about ninety, he was seized by a mob and died in prison in 177, one of the Martyrs of Lyon.
Bishop of the Gévaudan. Gregory of Tours says invading Alamanni beat him in his cave on Mont Mimat; he died of it.
Czech priest turned hermit on the Sázava river, then first abbot of the monastery that grew there. Canonized in 1204.
Chief man of Malta who hosted St. Paul after the shipwreck of Acts 28. Tradition makes him Malta's first bishop.
Bishop of Rodez, driven out by the Arian Visigoths for siding with Clovis. Later Bishop of Clermont; died c. 525.
Bishop of Siscia, now Sisak. Drowned at Savaria in 309 with a millstone at his neck; Prudentius says the stone floated.
Bishop of Carthage, friend of Augustine. Set adrift by the Vandal Gaiseric in unseaworthy ships; died exiled at Naples.
Abbot of Fulda, Archbishop of Mainz, called Teacher of Germany. Traditionally credited with the Veni Creator Spiritus.
Half-brother of St. Adalbert of Prague and his companion on the fatal Prussian mission. First Archbishop of Gniezno.
Maronite nun who prayed to share in Christ's sufferings, then lived for years in pain, blind and paralysed, until 1914.
Ministered in disguise as a peddler, musician and doctor during Mexico's persecution; later Bishop of Veracruz.
Engineer sent to Siberian hard labour after the 1863 uprising; later a Discalced Carmelite prior and confessor.
Widowed chanter of Toulouse who became a canon of Saint-Sernin, gave to the poor and helped build its basilica.
Canon regular from Durban in France, Bishop of Barbastro from 1104. Consecrated the Romanesque churches of Taüll.
Honored as the first Bishop of Senlis and evangelizer of its countryside. Often confused with St. Regulus of Arles.
Bishop of Gap from about 394, at the councils of Nîmes, Turin and Valence. Honored with his predecessor St. Tigidius.
Apostle of the Franks. As Bishop of Reims he baptized King Clovis, with some 3,000 Franks, around 496.
French Jesuit in China, beheaded with Fr. Modeste Andlauer by Boxers at Wuyi in 1900. A Martyr Saint of China.
Surgeon and Jesuit donné, killed in 1642 after teaching a Mohawk boy the sign of the cross. First North American Martyr.
Welsh schoolmaster and bard. Jailed for years as a recusant, then hanged, drawn and quartered at Wrexham in 1584.
Bishop of Chichester and canon lawyer. Credited with the prayer to know Christ more clearly, love him more dearly.
Empress, wife of Charles the Fat. Repudiated on a charge of adultery, she retired to Andlau, the abbey she founded.
Canon of Brioude who opened a hospice for the poor, then in 1043 founded the Benedictine abbey of La Chaise-Dieu.
Jesuit poet of The Burning Babe and hidden priest in London. Tortured by Topcliffe, hanged at Tyburn in 1595.
Asunción-born Jesuit, fluent in Guaraní, founder of mission towns on the Paraná and Uruguay. Killed at Caaró in 1628.
Pilgrim from Montpellier who nursed plague victims in Italy, caught the plague and was fed by a dog bringing bread.
Roman soldier won over by the confession of St. Lawrence and baptized by him; beaten with clubs and beheaded in 258.
Religious of the Sacred Heart on the American frontier. Potawatomi children called her Woman Who Prays Always.
Carthusian nun and prioress of La Celle-Roubaud. Food she carried to the poor is said to have turned into roses.
Priest of Barfleur, then Bishop of Coutances. Gregory of Tours says he buried the murdered Archbishop Praetextatus.
Bishop of Worms who preached to the Bavarians, then first Bishop of Salzburg. Restored St. Peter's and founded Nonnberg.
Monk of Lérins, then Bishop of Narbonne for some thirty years. Rebuilt a city church burned in 441.
Monks and bishops of Holy Island, from Aidan, who came from Iona in 635, to Cuthbert. Evangelizers of Northumbria.
Follower of Jesus who watched the Crucifixion and came with spices to the tomb on Easter morning (Mark 15:40; 16:1).
Lawyer turned monk, Bishop of Albi from 574. Stayed with his flock through famine and plague, which killed him in 584.
First Bishop of Toulouse, also called Sernin. Martyred by being tied to a bull and dragged to his death.
Hermit of Bigorre in the Pyrenees, honored at the Benedictine abbey that bore his name, Saint-Savin-en-Lavedan.
Monk who withdrew with St. Paternus to the Scissy forest on the Norman coast. Died the same day; both lie at Saint-Pair.
Founder of the monastery on Scattery Island in the Shannon estuary. Legend says he drove out its sea monster.
Bishop of Avranches in the 560s, after St. Paternus. Buried at Saint-Pair; Norman villages bear his name, Senier.
Bigorre landowner turned priest, praised by Gregory of Tours for his charity. Lilies at his tomb bloomed anew.
Apostle of Noricum. Fed the starving, ransomed captives and founded monasteries on the Danube as Rome's rule failed.
Shepherd from the Cotentin who became monk, abbot and Bishop of Avranches, then resigned to return to the monastic life.
Burgundian king who founded the abbey of Agaune. Had his son killed, repented, and was slain by the Franks in 524.
Archbishop of Warsaw exiled by the Tsar to Yaroslavl for 20 years. Founded the Franciscan Sisters of the Family of Mary.
Widowed young after a chaste marriage, she became a deaconess and abbess of Troclar, a convent near Albi.
Bernardine friar and preacher in Kraków, inspired by St. Bernardine of Siena. Died in 1482 nursing plague victims.
Son of a Frankish noble, abbot of Anisole (Saint-Calais) in Maine. Butler names him author of the Life of St. Calais.
Spokesman of the Scillitan martyrs, beheaded at Carthage in 180. Their Acts are the oldest dated Latin Church text.
Shepherd who became Bishop of Trimythous in Cyprus. Maimed in the Great Persecution; his relics rest in Corfu.
Canon Regular of Corpus Christi in Kraków. Preacher and confessor, called the Apostle of the Blessed Sacrament.
Polish noble who walked hundreds of miles from Vienna to become a Jesuit despite his father. Died a novice at 17.
Transylvanian Jesuit, a Martyr of Košice, tortured and beheaded by soldiers in 1619 for refusing to apostatize.
Irish princess of legend who fled to Norway. She and her companions died when a cave on Selja island fell on them.
Bishop of Winchester from 852. Folklore says rain on his feast, the day of his translation, means forty more days of it.
Bishop of Toulouse in the late 4th century. Began the basilica for St. Saturninus' relics, finished by St. Exuperius.
Virgin of the Rodez region in the 6th or 7th century, named in the Roman Martyrology and kept in the Rodez calendar.
Venerated in Gascony as an early bishop of Eauze and a martyr. His story survives only in late tradition.
Welsh monk-bishop of Llandaff and friend of St David. Founded Llandeilo Fawr and Penally; his tomb is at Llandaff.

saints.n: St. Teresa of Jesus Jornet Ibars
saints.bio: Catalan foundress of the Little Sisters of the Abandoned Elderly, devoted to caring for poor and forsaken old people.
Chilean Discalced Carmelite at Los Andes who died of typhus at 19, less than a year after entering. Chile's first saint.
Archbishop of Narbonne. Restored his cathedral after Moorish raids and worked to ransom Christian captives.
Merovingian princess, likely a daughter of Theuderic I, credited with founding Saint-Pierre-le-Vif abbey at Sens.
Greek monk from Tarsus, made Archbishop of Canterbury at 66. Organized the English Church and founded a famed school.
Franciscan priest from the Tarn, missionary in Shanxi. Killed by the Boxers at Taiyuan with Bishop Grassi, 9 July 1900.
Abbot and co-founder of the Kiev Caves Lavra, who brought the Studite cenobitic rule to the monks of Kievan Rus'.
First prior of Holy Cross in Coimbra, reformer of religious life in Portugal and the first Portuguese saint.
Co-founder of the Cenacle Sisters, pioneers of women's retreats. Removed as superior, she lived on in humble obedience.
Jesuit, nephew of Henry Garnet. Refused the Oath of Allegiance and died at Tyburn in 1608. One of the Forty Martyrs.
Japanese Dominican trained in Manila, sent to Formosa, then back to Japan in secret. Martyred at Nagasaki in 1634.
Augustinian friar, then Archbishop of Valencia. So lavish to the poor he was called the Almsgiver.
Bishop of Hamar, outlawed by King Eric II for defending the Church's rights. Died in exile at Ter Doest near Bruges.
Bishop of Skálholt from 1178, founder of Iceland's first Augustinian house. Patron of Iceland, honored on 23 December.
Early bishop of Gap in the Alps, commemorated with St Remedius in the Roman Martyrology on 3 February.
Saxon boy sold as a slave, freed and baptized by St Eligius. Monk of Solignac, missionary in Flanders, then a hermit.
Monk from Britain, abbot-bishop of Tréguier and one of the seven founding saints of Brittany.
Priest martyred at Ax in 452, by tradition. Ripoll's monks took his relics in 978; a fragment came back to Ax in 1886.
Bishop of Augsburg for 50 years who held the city against the Magyars in 955. First saint canonized by a pope (993).
Bishop of Rome 222-230 under Emperor Alexander Severus, a time of relative peace for the Church.
Chancellor to Queen Ultrogotha, then bishop of Cahors from the 580s. Known to us through Gregory of Tours.
Legendary British princess slain at Cologne with her fellow virgins. Patroness of Cologne; the Ursulines bear her name.
Catechist of King Clovis before his baptism, then by tradition first bishop of Arras, with oversight of Cambrai.
Missionary bishop in Raetia who ended his days as a hermit near Merano, dying in 475. An early patron of Passau.
Early bishop of Trier, called by tradition a disciple of St Peter sent to the Rhineland with Eucharius and Maternus.
Valerius, honored as the first bishop of Couserans. The church of Saint-Valier at Saint-Girons is dedicated to him.
Bishop of Cavaillon in Provence whose miracles are told by Gregory of Tours. Legend says he drove out a dragon.
Lector of St Justus of Lyon who followed his bishop into the Egyptian desert as a monk and died there, at Scetis.
African-born Bishop of Rome 189-199. Pressed the Roman date of Easter on the churches of Asia.
Martyr of Collioure on the Roussillon coast, commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 19 April.
Roman priest who founded the Union of Catholic Apostolate and the Pallottines. Seen as a forerunner of Catholic Action.
Bishop of Capsa who stood with Eugenius of Carthage against the Arian Vandals. Gregory of Tours says he was beheaded.
Irish monk known as the Geometer, Bishop of Salzburg and Apostle of Carinthia, who finished its first cathedral.
Norman hermit-preacher who founded Savigny Abbey and its congregation, later merged into the Cistercians.
Young Sicilian martyr in Lucania under Diocletian. One of the Fourteen Holy Helpers; St Vitus' dance bears his name.
Grand Prince of Kiev, baptized c. 988, who brought Christianity to the Rus'. Called Equal to the Apostles in the East.
Bishop of Tours driven from his see by the Arian Visigoths and exiled to Toulouse. Patron of Foix.
His wife taken from him, he became a monk and hermit, then founded the abbey near Boulogne now named Samer after him.
Anglo-Saxon nun who joined the mission of St Boniface; abbess of Heidenheim. Her 1 May translation gave Walpurgis Night.
Hermit and shepherd of the Saar country, by tradition abbot of Tholey. The town of St. Wendel bears his name.
Bishop of York who won the day for the Roman Easter at Whitby in 664. Exiled more than once; evangelized Sussex.
Canon and physician of Tours who gave his goods to the poor to live as a hermit and pilgrim. His relics rest at Mortain.
West Saxon pilgrim to Rome and the Holy Land, then co-worker of St Boniface and first bishop of Eichstätt.
Northumbrian monk, Apostle of the Frisians, first bishop of Utrecht and founder of Echternach Abbey.
Welsh virgin who, legend says, was beheaded for refusing a prince and raised by St Beuno. Her spring flows at Holywell.
Monk of British or Breton birth under St Bertin at Sithiu, who led the house at Wormhout in Flanders. Patron of millers.
Swabian monk, then bishop of Regensburg and tutor of the future Emperor Henry II. Reformer and tireless almsgiver.
Bishop of Worcester, the last Anglo-Saxon bishop to keep his see after 1066. Preached down the Bristol slave trade.
Catalan monk, abbot of Saint-Victor at Marseille and close friend of Odilo of Cluny. Rebuilt the abbey church.
Bohemian noblewoman, wife, mother and early lay Dominican. Fed the poor, sheltered refugees, founded a priory.
Priest of Lviv who served the poor, sick and abandoned, and founded the Sisters of St. Joseph in 1884.
Missionaries and Japanese faithful killed for Christ in 1617-1632 under the Tokugawa ban. Beatified in 1867.
Abbot of St Victor in Paris, then Bishop of Avranches from 1161. A Victorine preacher and loyal friend of Thomas Becket.
Shoemaker turned priest in Cologne. The Journeymen's Father, whose guilds grew into the worldwide Kolping Society.
Dominican prioress of Langeac and mystic who told Jean-Jacques Olier he would open France's first seminaries.
Superior of the canons of Chancelade, then Bishop of Cahors from 1636, visiting all 800 parishes at least nine times.
Brazilian farm girl of 12, killed in 1931 for resisting rape by her father's hired hand. Martyr of purity.
Archbishop of Zagreb and cardinal, convicted by Yugoslavia's communist regime in 1946. Died under house arrest in 1960.
Montreal-born priest of the diocese of Sens who refused the revolutionary oath. Killed at the Carmes in Paris, 1792.
Young Christian Worker from Roubaix, sent to Germany for forced labour, jailed for his Catholic activism. Died 1944.
Kraków housemaid and Franciscan tertiary who nursed wounded soldiers in WWI hospitals. Fell ill and died in 1922.
Lyon priest who founded the Prado to teach poor children and to form priests living poor among the poor.
Bishop of Płock from 1908. Arrested by the Nazis, he died in the Soldau camp at Działdowo in 1941, aged 83.
Curate of Calviac and Sainte-Mondane, diocese of Cahors. Died in 1794 on the Deux-Associés, a prison hulk off Rochefort.
Priest who refused the oath to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Killed in the September Massacres, Paris, 1792.
Dominican from Trogir, Bishop of Zagreb, then of Lucera, where he died in 1323 after being struck by an assailant.
Franciscan brother honored in Mexico's calendar, one of the 205 Martyrs of Japan. Killed for the faith in August 1627.
Priest imprisoned in Paris for refusing the revolutionary oath. Killed in the September Massacres of 1792.
French jurist made Patriarch of Aquileia in 1334. Murdered by rebel Friulian nobles in 1350.
One of St Dominic's first companions: prior at Toulouse, sent to Paris in 1217, then provincial of Provence. Died 1230.
Fr Guillaume Repin and 98 companions, priests, nuns and lay folk, mostly women, killed at Angers and Avrillé in 1793-94.
Priests of the English College at Douai, the college of the Douay-Rheims Bible, executed in England 1577-1680.
191 bishops, priests, religious and laymen killed in Paris prisons in the September Massacres of 1792.
Ten martyrs linked to Sussex, six priests and four laymen, who died for the Catholic faith across five English reigns.
32 nuns, Ursulines, Sacramentines, Cistercians and a Benedictine, guillotined at Orange in July 1794.
Archbishop of Gniezno who founded a Cistercian abbey, then resigned his see to live out his days as a hermit.
Founded the Missionary Sisters of the Holy Family in 1905 and worked in St Petersburg until 1921. Died in Białystok.
Norbertine nun at Zwierzyniec in Kraków and cousin of St Hyacinth. A life hidden in prayer; died in 1259.
Polish priest who joined Don Bosco's Salesians, then founded the Michaelites (Congregation of St Michael the Archangel).
Puerto Rican lay catechist, Charlie to his friends, who championed liturgical renewal and the Easter Vigil.
Peasant girl of 16 from near Tarnów, killed in 1914 by a Russian soldier as she resisted rape.
Catinon Menette, Dominican tertiary and lacemaker of Mauriac who hid priests and led them by night in the Revolution.
El Pelé, Romani mule dealer of Barbastro. Shot in 1936 for defending a priest and refusing to give up his rosary.
Silesian Dominican and kinsman of St Hyacinth. Tradition credits his prayer with saving Wrocław from the Mongols.
Rodez science teacher who flew a hot-air balloon in 1784 and explored caves. Killed at Saint-Firmin, Paris, 1792.
Sulpician priest from Mayenne, seminary director at Bourges. Died in 1794 on a prison hulk off Rochefort.
Last Emperor of Austria and King of Hungary. Sought peace in WWI; died in exile on Madeira in 1922.
Duke of Brittany who wore a hair shirt under his armour. Killed at the Battle of Auray in 1364.
Genoese Jesuit who taught mathematics and astronomy in Kyoto. Burned at Nagasaki in the Great Martyrdom of 1622.
Parish priest who joined St Francis in 1215, went with the first friars to Aquitaine and served lepers. Died at Cahors.
French Jesuit priest who refused the revolutionary oath. Killed in the September Massacres in Paris, 1792, aged 67.
Dublin-born Benedictine, third Abbot of Maredsous, whose Christ, the Life of the Soul became a spiritual classic.
Spiritan missionary in Senegal and WWI chaplain who built up the Orphan Apprentices of Auteuil for poor boys.
Quebec pianist turned Religious of Jesus and Mary. Mystic of union with Christ; died in 1929 at 32.
Italian Passionist missionary to England who received John Henry Newman into the Catholic Church in 1845.
Polish layman who served the rural poor with orphanages and libraries and founded the Servant Sisters.
Widowed Waterford merchant who founded the Christian Brothers and the Presentation Brothers to school poor boys.
Flemish priest and apostle of the Eucharist who urged frequent Communion and founded a Eucharistic League for children.
Montreal widow who lost husband and children, served the poor, and founded the Sisters of Providence. Died of cholera.
Canon of Esztergom turned hermit in the Pilis hills. Founded the Pauline Fathers, the Order of St Paul the First Hermit.
Vicar general of Castres. Deported for his faith to the prison hulks of Rochefort, where he died in 1794.
Bavarian Redemptorist in America. Pastor and preacher of parish missions; died of yellow fever in New Orleans, 1867.
Basque priest from Isturits, confessor at the Collège Sainte-Barbe in Paris. Killed at the Carmes, 2 September 1792.
Bishop of Beauvais. Killed at the Carmes in Paris in September 1792, alongside his brother, the Bishop of Saintes.
Priest from Vitrac in Auvergne, vicar general of Clermont. Killed at the Carmes in Paris, 2 September 1792.
Alsatian priest from Neuf-Brisach, canon of Saint-Lizier. Killed at the Carmes in Paris, 2 September 1792.
Franciscan from French Flanders. Served the Custody of the Holy Land, then promoted the Notre-Dame-du-Cap shrine.
Sorbonne scholar, husband and father. Co-founded the Society of St Vincent de Paul in 1833 to serve the poor of Paris.
Sicilian Franciscan in China and Hong Kong. Founded the Studium Biblicum and gave Chinese Catholics a complete Bible.
Secretly revived the Marian Fathers under tsarist rule. Bishop of Vilnius 1918-1925, then papal visitor to Lithuania.
Young noble of Lunel who became a hermit and pilgrim. Died on pilgrimage at Monte Santo in the Marche, 1298.
First Queen of Hungary, wife of St Stephen and sister of Emperor St Henry II. Ended her days as abbess in Passau.
Sailor from the Bay of Kotor who, moved by a sermon at about 30, became an Augustinian religious. Died at Murano.
Elected after a near three-year vacancy. Called the Second Council of Lyon and created the conclave with Ubi periculum.
Portuguese priest, pilgrim to Rome and Jerusalem, Dominican hermit. Built the bridge over the Tâmega at Amarante.
Augustinian friar from the Algarve. Preacher, catechist of children, scribe of choir books; prior at Torres Vedras.
Swedish-born Bishop of Turku for 28 years. Friend and envoy of St Bridget; founded a school and a hospital.
Dominican mystic who studied under Meister Eckhart at Cologne. Called himself the Servant of Eternal Wisdom.
Capuchin confessor under tsarist suppression. Founded hidden religious congregations that lived without habits.
Orthodox-born shepherdess turned Catholic anchoress, walled in a cell at Kotor. Dominican tertiary and peacemaker.
Bohemian noble who founded Teplá Abbey and became a Premonstratensian. Seized by enemies, he refused ransom and starved.
Jesuit from Porto leading a mission to Brazil. He and 39 companions were killed by Huguenot corsairs off La Palma, 1570.
Maltese lawyer in minor orders who declined priesthood. Taught the faith to children and British soldiers and sailors.
Peter of Tarentaise: Dominican theologian at Paris and Archbishop of Lyon. Elected pope in 1276, he reigned five months.
Benedetto Odescalchi of Como. Reforming pope who curbed nepotism and backed the relief of Vienna and the Holy League.
Sister of St Louis IX. Refused royal marriages and founded the Franciscan abbey of Longchamp, living beside it.
Salesian brother and printer who worked with youth. Arrested under communism and executed in Budapest, 1953.
Croatian layman from Banja Luka. Teacher, liturgical pioneer and co-founder of the Catholic youth Eagles. Died at 31.
Eudist priest from Vire who headed the seminary at Caen and wrote against the Revolution. Killed at the Carmes, 1792.
Former Jesuit born in Saint-Domingue, vicar general of Lyon. Refused the Civil Constitution; killed at the Carmes, 1792.
Priest of Anjou, born at Rochefort-sur-Loire. Guillotined at Angers during the Terror, 5 January 1794.
Franciscan friar made Archbishop of Halych in 1391. Built churches, schools and hospitals; died at Lviv in 1409.
Sulpician priest from Embrun, superior of the clerics of Saint-Sulpice. Killed at the Carmes in Paris, 2 September 1792.
Former Jesuit priest who refused the revolutionary oath. Killed in the September Massacres in Paris, 3 September 1792.
Parish priest of La Trinité in Laval who refused the revolutionary oath. Guillotined with 13 other priests, 1794.
White Father from Angers. Killed at the Tizi Ouzou mission in Algeria with three confreres, December 1994.
Painter who became a Jesuit brother and sailed for Brazil with Ignatius de Azevedo. Killed by corsairs at sea, 1570.
Priest who refused the revolutionary oath. Killed in the September Massacres in Paris, 3 September 1792.
Priest from Ginestas in the diocese of Narbonne. Killed at the Carmes in Paris for his faith, 2 September 1792.
Priest from the diocese of Rodez, chaplain of the Pitié hospital in Paris. Killed at the Carmes, 2 September 1792.
Archbishop of Arles who refused the Civil Constitution. Heads the roll of the martyrs of September 1792 at the Carmes.
Priest from Angers, parish priest of Saint-Doucelin at Allonnes. Killed at the Carmes in Paris, 2 September 1792.
Sicilian Jesuit in Japan, first European to reach Hokkaido. Gave himself up and was burned alive at Edo in 1623.
Princess and onetime regent of Portugal who refused royal suitors and lived in the Dominican convent at Aveiro.
Polish Jesuit teacher who left for Madagascar at 48 to serve lepers. Built the leper hospital at Marana.
Young Cistercian priest and beloved youth chaplain. Lured out on a false sick call and murdered at 25, 1957.
Lorraine priest who founded the Sisters of Providence, served a decade in Sichuan, and died nursing the sick at Trier.
Pupil of Ivo of Chartres, Bishop of Thérouanne for 31 years. Reformer who forgave the men who tried to kill him.
Bishop of Satu Mare who refused to break with Rome. Tortured and died in Jilava prison under communism, 1952.
De La Salle Brother, in religion Br. Jacob Samuel. Killed in Spain in August 1936 during the Civil War; beatified 2007.
De La Salle Brother, in religion Br. Louis de Jésus. Killed in Spain in July 1936 during the Civil War; beatified 2007.
Trappist of Sainte-Marie du Désert who struggled with learning, was ordained a priest, and died of tuberculosis at 25.
Bernardine Franciscan friar of Warsaw. Fiery preacher and early Polish-language hymn writer, devoted to the Passion.
Hungarian prince and eye surgeon, the 'doctor of the poor', who treated poor patients free of charge. Father of 13.
Chilean girl at a Salesian school in Argentina. Offered her life for her mother's conversion; died at 12.
First exarch of the Russian Greek Catholic Church. Studite monk, Solovki prisoner, died in Soviet exile in 1935.
Priest and educator from Quillan. Founded the Sisters of the Guardian Angel to teach children; died in Gijón.
Scout from Dunkirk, one of the 50 martyrs of the secret apostolate to French forced labourers. Died at Buchenwald, 1945.
Priest of Bayonne who sheltered poor and abandoned girls. With his sister he founded the Servants of Mary in 1842.
Dominican missionary in the Philippines. Seized at sea with Peter de Zúñiga en route to Japan; burned alive at Nagasaki.
Priest who refused the Revolution's clerical oath. Killed in the September Massacres in Paris, 3 September 1792.
Bishop of Saint-Hyacinthe, Quebec, 1875-1901. Founded the Sisters of Saint Martha; co-founded the Sisters of St Joseph.
Portuguese infanta, briefly Queen of Castile. After her marriage was annulled, lived as a Cistercian nun at Arouca.
Young Christian Worker from Rennes. Sent to Germany for forced labour; arrested for his apostolate, died at Mauthausen.
Polish widow and mother. Co-founded the Sisters of the Immaculate Conception; schooled girls at Jazłowiec.
Duchess of Alençon. As a widow she ruled her duchy and protected the poor; ended her days a Poor Clare at Argentan.
Quebec teacher who founded the Sisters of Saint Anne in 1850. Removed as superior, she served for decades in obscurity.
Co-founded the Sisters of the Holy Names of Jesus and Mary at Longueuil to educate girls. Died at 38.
Norman sister of St Marie-Madeleine Postel's congregation. Holiness in humble daily work at Saint-Sauveur-le-Vicomte.
Naples-born heiress who became a Benedictine nun at Mdina, Malta. Abbess, mystic and friend of the poor.
Founded the Felician Sisters in Warsaw in 1855. Franciscan care for orphans, the poor and the sick.
Italian Franciscan Missionary of Mary. Humble worker sent to China; died of typhus in Shanxi at 26.
Norman Augustinian nursing sister at Quebec's Hôtel-Dieu from age 16. Mystic of New France; died at 36.

saints.n: Bl. Mary of Jesus Crucified Petković
saints.bio: Croatian from Korčula who founded the Daughters of Mercy. Served the poor in Croatia and Latin America.

saints.n: Bl. Mary of Jesus the Good Shepherd Siedliska
saints.bio: Polish noblewoman who founded the Sisters of the Holy Family of Nazareth in Rome, 1875, and sent them to America.

saints.n: Bl. Mary of the Incarnation (Madame Acarie)
saints.bio: Parisian wife, mother and mystic. Brought Teresa's Discalced Carmel to France; died a Carmelite lay sister.
Founded the Helpers of the Holy Souls in Paris in 1856. Served the poor and sick for the souls in purgatory.
Founded the Society of Mary Auxiliatrix. Expelled from her own congregation, she died a humble nun elsewhere.
Superior of the Nazareth Sisters at Nowogródek. Offered her life for jailed townsmen; shot by the Nazis with 10 sisters.
Polish countess who founded the Missionary Sisters of St Peter Claver to support the Catholic missions in Africa.
Spanish catechist from Almería who served Madrid's slum dwellers and workers. Founded the Catechetical Institute, 1901.
Swiss canon of the Great St Bernard. Missionary on the Tibetan border; shot at the Choula pass in 1949.
Auxiliary bishop of Włocławek. Arrested by the Gestapo in 1939; died at Dachau in 1943.
Mexican Jesuit, a priest in disguise under the Calles persecution. Shot in 1927 crying '¡Viva Cristo Rey!'
Minim friar from Amiens. Founded free schools for poor children and the Sisters of the Infant Jesus.
Danish anatomist and a founder of geology. Became a Catholic in Florence, then a bishop for the Nordic missions.
Parish priest of Le Louroux-Béconnais. Refused the oath, served in hiding; guillotined at Angers in his vestments.
First Ukrainian Catholic bishop in Canada. Arrested by the Soviets in 1945; died in a Karaganda gulag.
Franciscan friar from Friuli. Traveled through India and Sumatra to Beijing; dictated a famous travel account.
Ukrainian Greek Catholic priest jailed for refusing Orthodoxy. Roving missionary in Kazakhstan; died in Dolinka camp.
First Christian hermit, per St Jerome. Decades alone in the Egyptian desert; buried by St Anthony.
Basilian monk and Greek Catholic bishop of Prešov. Refused to join Orthodoxy; died in Leopoldov prison, 1960.
Norbertine canon of Blanchelande who told the truth at his trial though it cost his life. Guillotined at Coutances.
Seville-born Augustinian, son of a viceroy of New Spain. Seized at sea bound for Japan, 1620; burned alive at Nagasaki.
Japanese Jesuit who walked overland to Jerusalem and Rome, then went home to persecuted Japan. Martyred in 1639.
Cistercian papal legate sent against the Cathars. His murder in 1208 triggered the Albigensian Crusade.
Made Bishop of Metz and cardinal at 14 by the Avignon pope. Austere, prayerful youth who died at 17 near Avignon.
Catechist of New Britain, husband and father. Defended marriage under Japanese occupation; killed in prison, 1945.
Algiers-born Dominican, bishop of Oran. Voice of Christian-Muslim friendship; killed by a bomb in 1996 with his driver.
Non-juring priest who revived the Good Saviour Sisters of Caen, opened a school for the deaf, and led Caen's university.
Priest who refused the revolutionary oath. Killed in the September Massacres in Paris, 3 September 1792.
Longest-reigning pope since St Peter, 1846-1878. Defined the Immaculate Conception, convened Vatican I, lost Rome.
Norman nun who succeeded St. Marie-Madeleine Postel as superior general for 30 years and led relief in the 1870 war.
Hermit of the Craon forest with Robert of Arbrissel, then founder of the double abbey of Saint-Sulpice near Rennes.
Cavalry officer turned Conventual Franciscan. Plain preacher and confessor who fed the poor and nursed epidemic victims.
Priest of Albi who ministered in secret to French forced labourers in Germany. Died at Buchenwald in 1944.
Archdeacon cut down with the inquisitors William Arnaud and Stephen of Saint-Thibéry at Avignonet castle in May 1242.
Canon lawyer and dean of Saint-Aignan in Orléans who joined St Dominic. His preaching drew many at Bologna and Paris.
Breton hermit and wandering preacher who founded Fontevraud, a double abbey of monks and nuns ruled by an abbess.
Daughter of Charity who served the poor of Paris's Mouffetard district for 54 years and mentored Frédéric Ozanam.
Polish princess wed as a child to Coloman of Galicia. Widowed in 1241, she became a Poor Clare at Zawichost and Skała.
Infanta of Portugal, Lady of Alenquer. Welcomed the Franciscan protomartyrs and founded Celas convent near Coimbra.
Sister of Social Service who sheltered Jews in Budapest. Shot by the Arrow Cross on the Danube bank in December 1944.
Hermit who lived in a cave in Luxembourg's Grünewald on wild plants and stream water. Visited by Achard of Clairvaux.
Galician rancher and road builder in New Spain who became a Franciscan lay brother at 72 and begged for the friars.
Secretly consecrated bishop in Communist Romania in 1949. Refused to break with Rome and died in Aiud Prison.
Portuguese princess and Queen of León. After her marriage was annulled she made Lorvão Cistercian and took the veil.
Greek Catholic Bishop of Mukachevo who refused to break with the Pope under Soviet rule. Murdered by the NKVD at 36.
Village schoolmaster of Biville turned priest. Preached, taught the catechism and tended the sick across Normandy.
Alsatian Dominican, Father Thomas, jailed for preaching during the Terror. Died on the prison hulks of Rochefort.
Priest from Laval, parish priest of Barville in the diocese of Orléans. Killed at the Carmes in Paris, 2 September 1792.
Cluniac monk and pope from 1088. Built up the Roman Curia and launched the First Crusade at Clermont in 1095.
Benedictine abbot elected pope at Avignon. Kept the Rule as pope and brought the papacy back to Rome for three years.
Redemptorist made a secret bishop in Soviet Ukraine. Jailed twice, exiled in 1972, died of his injuries in Winnipeg.
Bishop of Kraków and author of the Chronica Polonorum. Resigned in 1218 to live as a Cistercian monk at Jędrzejów.
Greek Catholic layman and husband, shot by tsarist troops in 1874 while defending the church at Pratulin with 12 others.
Romanian prince and diplomat turned Catholic priest. Opened Bucharest's first free clinic; died in a Communist prison.
Bishop of Győr who spoke up for persecuted Jews. Shot by Soviet soldiers in 1945 while shielding women in his home.
Michaelite priest who ran a secret school for seminarians. Died in Gross-Rosen, pushed into the camp quarry in 1944.
Hungarian princess, wife of Bolesław the Pious. Widowed, she became a Poor Clare and founded the convent at Gniezno.
Holy Cross Sister and X-ray nurse in Bratislava, tortured and jailed for helping priests flee the Communists.
Son of a Mapuche chief and Salesian pupil who hoped to be a priest. Died of tuberculosis in Rome at 18.
Auxiliary bishop of Esztergom, arrested days after taking charge of the archdiocese in 1950. Died in Kistarcsa camp.

extra.bio: Byzantine Archbishop of Ohrid whose Gospel commentaries distil Chrysostom and the Greek Fathers.
Alexandrian scholar and exegete who compiled the Hexapla. Never canonized; his teachings were condemned in 553.
Works once credited to St John Chrysostom: the Opus Imperfectum on Matthew and Victor of Antioch on Mark.
The standard medieval marginal and interlinear Bible commentary, gathered from the Fathers at Laon.
Benedictine monk who taught at Auxerre, Reims and Paris. Commented on Scripture and the liberal arts.
Writings that circulated under St Jerome's name but are by other, mostly unknown, authors.
Scholar of York who led Charlemagne's palace school, then abbot of St Martin's at Tours.
Aquinas's label for unnamed Greek commentators drawn from Byzantine catenae on the Gospels.
Bishop of Nyssa, younger brother of Basil the Great. Mystical theologian; wrote the Life of Moses.
Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine and father of church history. Wrote the Ecclesiastical History.
Bishop of Bostra in Arabia under Julian the Apostate. Wrote Against the Manichaeans.
Sermons and treatises once ascribed to St Augustine but written by other, often unknown, authors.
Byzantine monk who defended Christ's two wills against the Monothelites; his tongue and hand were cut off.
Carolingian homilist. Works long credited to Haymo of Halberstadt; many are now given to Haimo of Auxerre.
Egyptian monk and priest near Pelusium. About two thousand of his letters, many on Scripture, survive.
Blind teacher of Alexandria and defender of Nicaea. Never canonized; condemned with Origen and Evagrius in 553.
Bishop of Salamis in Cyprus. Catalogued and refuted the heresies of his day in the Panarion.
Third ecumenical council. Condemned Nestorius and proclaimed Mary Theotokos, Mother of God.
Bishop of Ancyra who opposed Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus (431), where his homilies were read.
Anonymous 4th-century Roman commentator on St Paul whose work long circulated under St Ambrose's name.
Works once ascribed to St Athanasius; the Catena excerpts come from Vigilius of Thapsus.
Christian teacher in Alexandria. Wrote the Exhortation to the Heathen, the Instructor and the Stromata.
Pupil of Origen and Bishop of Alexandria, called the Great. A confessor under Decius and Valerian.
Priest of Marseille. Continued Jerome's Lives of Illustrious Men; wrote On Church Dogmas.
Spanish Jewish convert, baptized in 1106. Wrote the Dialogue against the Jews and the Disciplina Clericalis.
Fifth ecumenical council, convened under Justinian. Condemned the Three Chapters.
Jewish priest and historian of the first century. Wrote The Jewish War and the Antiquities of the Jews.
Monk and abbot of Corbie. His treatise On the Body and Blood of the Lord taught the Real Presence.
Prior of Bec, then Archbishop of Canterbury from 1070. Defended the Real Presence against Berengar.
Bishop of Emesa in Syria. Wrote On the Nature of Man, joining Greek philosophy with Christian faith.
Master of the cathedral school of Laon and a founder of the Glossa Ordinaria. Not St Anselm of Canterbury.
Carthaginian apologist who coined much Latin theological vocabulary. Later joined the Montanists.
Syriac bishop of Mabbug and ascetic writer. Opposed the Council of Chalcedon; not in communion with Rome.
Alexandrian merchant and traveller who wrote the Christian Topography, a Bible-based account of the world.
The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles: an early church manual on morals, baptism, the Eucharist and ministry.
Early writings once attributed to St. Ignatius of Antioch, now known to be by other authors.
Early writings once attributed to St. Clement of Rome, now known to be by other authors.
Early writings once attributed to Tertullian, now known to be by other authors.
Early writings once attributed to St. Cyprian, now known to be by other authors.
Franciscan friar and missionary preacher in Italy who set up the Stations of the Cross in hundreds of places.
Ninth abbot of Iona. Wrote the Life of St Columba and the Law of Innocents protecting non-combatants.
Genoese laywoman, mystic and hospital administrator, remembered for her Treatise on Purgatory.
Bishop of Tours and historian of the Franks. Wrote the History of the Franks and lives of the saints.
The Wonderworker. Pupil of Origen, then Bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus.
Bishop and martyr, critic of Origen's teaching. Wrote the Banquet of the Ten Virgins.
Bishop of Alexandria, beheaded in 311. Wrote canons on readmitting those who lapsed in persecution.
Monk of Lérins. His Commonitorium names the faith held everywhere, always and by all.
